The Tuesday Table

Every Tuesday morning I sit at the long table in the Mechanicsburg public library, under the window that leaks cold air in January, and somebody sits down across from me with a stack of envelopes.

It’s always the same stack. A glossy one from an insurance company showing two people on bicycles. A thin one from Social Security. Three nearly identical booklets from plans the person has never heard of. A postcard with ACT NOW printed in red. And underneath all of it, still sealed, the gray-and-blue “Medicare & You” handbook that arrived in September.

Last fall a man in a Penn State windbreaker set his pile down, pushed it two inches toward me, and said, “Just tell me which one.”

I didn’t. I never do. It isn’t modesty.

Two questions, and only you have the answers

Here is the part the television ads leave out. There is no best Medicare plan. There is only the plan that fits one particular person’s doctors, prescriptions, travel habits and tolerance for a bad year.

Let me put it on the board.

  1. Which doctors, hospitals and pharmacies do you need to keep?
  2. How much money could you hand over in a year when something goes seriously wrong, without it wrecking you?

I can explain every rule in the program. I cannot answer those two questions for you, and until they’re answered, every piece of advice anybody gives you is a guess wearing a suit.

The man in the windbreaker turned out to have a cardiologist in Hershey he’d been seeing for eleven years and a daughter in Oregon he visits for a month each summer. Those two facts narrowed his real choices faster than any brochure on the table. We spent most of the hour on his doctor list, not on premiums.

That’s the whole method of this book. Answer the two questions, then let the rules tell you what’s possible.

Why I taught this to myself

I taught civics and American government at a Cumberland County high school for 34 years. Thirty-four years of explaining to teenagers why a law says what it says, and why the sentence is so long.

Then I turned 65, my district’s retiree health coverage ended, and I discovered that knowing how a bill becomes a law teaches you nothing about Part B.

Joan sat beside me at our kitchen table reading drug names off a pharmacy printout while I clicked through screens. We got through it. I also got stubborn about it, in the way retired teachers do, and read the handbook cover to cover, then the Social Security Administration’s own explainers, then the handbook again. Neighbors started asking. The library table came after that.

I have no insurance license. I’ve never sold a policy, I don’t get paid when you pick a plan, and I’d be useless to an insurance company because I keep telling people to check the plan’s own documents instead of its commercials. My strong opinion, built one Tuesday at a time: afternoon television and brother-in-law advice cause more bad Medicare decisions than the rules ever have.

Why this book says 2026 when the cover says 2027

Before you price a 2027 plan, check which year’s numbers are printed here.

Medicare’s dollar amounts change every single year. The Part A and Part B premiums, the deductibles, the yearly cap on what you pay for prescriptions, the income thresholds that raise your premium if you earned above them. All of it is re-set annually by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, with the income-related amounts published by Social Security.

CMS and SSA publish the next year’s amounts in the fall, but the release date varies. Check the official cost pages before you act on any number. I’m not going to promise you a date on an agency’s behalf, and nobody else should either.

Some 2027 Part D amounts are already published and identified as 2027 in Chapters 4 and 9; where CMS or SSA has not yet posted 2027 amounts, this book uses clearly labeled 2026 figures. Check official figures again before enrolling.

Use Chapter 9 to replace the dated federal figures; then separately verify current plan documents, formularies, provider networks and state rules before choosing coverage. A penciled number does not update the rest of the book.

The rules themselves move far more slowly than the prices. A seven-month enrollment window is still seven months. The reason a late penalty exists hasn’t changed since Congress wrote it. Learn the structure from these pages, then verify the dollars at the source.

The order things happen in

Medicare isn’t one decision. It’s a sequence, and the sequence has a brutal feature: some of its doors only open once.

So the chapters follow the order a real person meets these choices, not alphabetical order and not the order an insurance glossary would use.

First, what Parts A, B, C and D actually are, because almost every conversation at my table starts with a misunderstanding about one of the four. Then enrollment timing and the penalties for missing it, which is the chapter I’d read tonight if you’re anywhere near 65. Then the big fork: Original Medicare with a Medigap policy, or a Medicare Advantage plan. Then prescription coverage and how to compare plans on total yearly cost rather than the monthly premium, which is where most of the money hides. Then Medigap and its one-time window. Then the income-related surcharge called IRMAA, which catches people by surprise because it looks back at a tax return from two years earlier. Then the help available at the other end of the income scale, which far more people qualify for than claim. Then working past 65, and the employer-coverage traps that come with it.

Every substantive chapter ends with a checklist, a worksheet or a decision rule you can carry to medicare.gov’s Plan Finder or to a counselor. They’re meant to be written on.

You can read this straight through in an evening or two. If you’re short on time, read the enrollment chapter and the one on your own live question, then come back for the rest before the fall.

One boundary. People ask me at the same table when they should claim Social Security, and it’s a different decision with different math, so it gets its own book: Social Security, Claimed On Purpose. Here I’ll stay on Medicare.

Where to get help that isn’t me

I can tell you how the rules work. I can’t look at your situation, and neither can a book.

Three places can, and none of them earn a commission. Medicare’s own line, 1-800-MEDICARE, is staffed year-round. Every state runs a State Health Insurance Assistance Program, usually called SHIP; in Pennsylvania ours is APPRISE. SHIP counselors offer free, unbiased one-on-one Medicare counseling; find your local program at shiphelp.org. And medicare.gov’s Plan Finder will do arithmetic that no brochure wants you to do.

Call a licensed agent or a tax professional when the stakes outgrow a checklist. A premium surcharge landing the year after you retire is one of those moments. So is weighing an employer plan against Medicare with a spouse’s coverage in the mix, or facing a health condition that could let a Medigap insurer turn you down. Pay someone who can look at your actual numbers. I’ll flag those moments as we reach them.

A few rules also vary by state, and the three states that standardize Medigap differently will get named where it matters. When something depends on where you live, I’ll say so rather than let you assume Pennsylvania’s answer is yours.

That’s the rule. You don’t have to like it.

Before you turn the page

Go find the envelopes. The glossy ones, the booklet, the postcard with the red lettering, whatever came in the mail and got moved to the counter so you could eat dinner.

Put them in one pile, somewhere you’ll see it. Then get a pencil, because the worksheets in here don’t work in your head.

The man in the windbreaker kept his pile in a canvas tote bag hanging on the back of a kitchen chair. He said it annoyed him into dealing with it. Good enough.

Chapter 1: Four Letters, but Not Four Add-ons

I keep one sheet of paper in the folder I bring to the library. Four letters down the left margin, in pencil, one word beside each. A, hospital. B, doctor. C, delivery. D, drugs.

That sheet exists because of a question I get more than any other, usually phrased exactly this way: “So do I buy B, or do I buy C?”

Fair question. There’s a wrong idea buried in it, though, and the wrong idea is expensive.

Medicare has four parts, but they don’t sit in a row like items on a menu. Parts A and B make up Original Medicare. Part C is another way to receive those benefits, usually with Part D included. Part D covers outpatient prescription drugs. Until the shape is clear, every comparison you try to make is a comparison between things that aren’t comparable, and you’ll feel stupid for being confused when the fault is in the naming.

So. Letters.

A is the hospital part, and its deductible works oddly

Part A covers inpatient care in hospitals, skilled nursing facility care, hospice care, and home health care. That’s Medicare.gov’s own list of what it helps pay for, and the word carrying the weight is inpatient.

Most people pay no monthly premium for Part A. Medicare.gov says it’s $0 for most people, because they or a spouse paid Medicare taxes long enough while working, generally at least ten years. If you don’t have that work record, you may be able to buy Part A, and in 2026 the buy-in premium is either $311 or $565 a month depending on how long you or your spouse paid in, according to Medicare.gov’s cost pages. Those are 2026 amounts. Check the current one before you budget around it.

Premium-free doesn’t mean free. Here’s where people get hurt.

In 2026, Medicare.gov puts the Part A deductible at $1,736, and you pay it for each inpatient hospital benefit period, not once a year. Read that sentence twice. Your Part B deductible is annual, your Part A deductible is per benefit period, and Medicare.gov states plainly that there’s no limit to the number of benefit periods you can have in a year. Two separate hospital admissions far enough apart, and you can pay that deductible twice in the same calendar year.

How the clock on a benefit period starts and stops is its own small piece of arithmetic, and Medicare.gov has a page explaining it, linked right from the cost table. Look it up when it matters to you. What you need in your head now is just this: Part A’s big number can repeat.

After the deductible, Part A’s 2026 inpatient hospital schedule runs like this, per Medicare.gov. Days 1 through 60 cost you nothing more. Days 61 through 90 cost $434 each day. Days 91 through 150 cost $868 each day, while you spend down the 60 lifetime reserve days you get once in your life. After day 150, you pay everything.

Skilled nursing care has its own ladder. In 2026, Medicare.gov lists days 1 through 20 at $0 after the Part A deductible, days 21 through 100 at $217 each day, and everything after day 100 on you. Part A limits that coverage to 100 days per benefit period.

And one trap worth a paragraph of its own, because it has blindsided people I’ve sat with. Medicare generally covers a skilled nursing stay only after a qualifying inpatient hospital stay of at least three days in a row. Medicare.gov says time spent under observation or in the emergency room before you’re admitted doesn’t count toward those three days, even if you were there overnight. You can sleep in a hospital bed for two nights, be billed as an outpatient, and fail the test. If you or a parent is in a hospital and somebody mentions rehab afterward, ask the question out loud: am I admitted as an inpatient, or under observation? Also ask the hospital and your plan whether an approved ACO or Medicare Advantage three-day-stay waiver applies; other SNF eligibility requirements still matter. Write down the answer and the date.

Hospice is the gentlest part of Part A’s cost structure. For 2026, Medicare.gov lists $0 for covered hospice services, up to $5 per qualifying home pain-or-symptom prescription, and 5% of the approved amount for inpatient respite; verify the coverage-year amounts before relying on them.

The bed does not decide which part pays

A hospital wristband tells you where you are. It does not establish inpatient coverage. That difference matters before a bill arrives because the admission status can affect the next place you receive care.

On Medicare.gov’s inpatient and outpatient status page, inpatient status begins with formal admission under a doctor’s order. Until that happens, emergency department care and observation are outpatient services, even if you stay overnight. The page tells you or your caregiver to ask about your status each day. Do that while the hospital can still explain the order, not from the kitchen six weeks later.

The official page supplies a useful contrast: an emergency visit followed by a formal admission is not the same as outpatient surgery followed by an overnight stay without an admission order. The first can bring an inpatient hospital benefit into the picture. The second remains outpatient. How ill you felt and how many hours you spent waiting cannot settle that distinction on their own.

If observation lasts more than 24 hours, the hospital must provide a Medicare Outpatient Observation Notice, called the MOON, according to Medicare.gov. It explains the observation status and its possible cost consequences. The initials sound like something a retired science teacher would explain. Here they mean you should read the page before agreeing that you understand it. Ask what status applies now and whether it changed during the stay.

There can also be two parts paying for one inpatient episode. Medicare.gov’s inpatient-care page says Part B generally covers the doctor’s services during a hospital stay. Part A’s hospital schedule is therefore not a price for every professional service connected with that admission. When estimating a planned stay, ask the hospital which charges are facility charges and which may arrive from clinicians. Do not assume a hospital deductible absorbs a separate physician bill.

For the skilled nursing question introduced above, the discharge day does not count toward the qualifying three-day inpatient stay, Medicare.gov says. Nor does observation time before admission. That makes the admission order’s date important. Ask the discharge planner to explain how the actual dates satisfy the rule or how an approved waiver applies; do not count nights yourself and declare the question settled.

The same SNF coverage page requires more than those dates. It names remaining benefit-period days, admission to the SNF generally within 30 days after leaving the hospital, daily skilled-care need, and a Medicare-certified facility. The required care must relate to a condition treated during the qualifying stay or a new condition arising while receiving SNF care for that condition. These are eligibility conditions, not a promise that a reserved bed comes with Medicare payment.

Skilled care can be needed to improve a condition, maintain it, or prevent or slow deterioration, the page explains. Do not translate “rehab” into “coverage only while improvement is visible.” The treating team must assess the skilled need. Conversely, needing a place to recover or help with everyday tasks does not by itself establish the Medicare skilled-care benefit. Have the team identify the benefit being requested and who will provide the qualifying care.

Home health does not mean someone stays all day

The words home health can make a household imagine a much larger service than the Medicare benefit provides. A nurse visiting to manage a wound is a different arrangement from someone remaining in the house whenever a spouse goes out.

Medicare.gov’s home health coverage page ties eligibility to being homebound and needing part-time or intermittent skilled services. Its homebound definition concerns difficulty leaving because of illness or injury, the help needed to leave, and the considerable effort involved. It does not mean you are forbidden to leave for medical treatment or short, infrequent non-medical absences. The page also says adult day care attendance does not automatically prevent home health care.

A clinician must see you in person, confirm the need, and order the care; a Medicare-certified agency must provide it. Covered services can include skilled nursing and qualifying therapies. Home health aide help is tied to receiving the specified skilled services, not an independent promise of ongoing bathing or housekeeping assistance for anyone with Medicare.

The official exclusions are the boundary a family should see before making a schedule. Medicare does not pay under this benefit for round-the-clock home care, delivered meals, shopping or cleaning unrelated to the care plan, or personal care when that is the only care needed. If the discharge plan assumes someone will help at night, ask who that person is and how the service will be paid for. An agency’s visit schedule cannot stand in for the hours no visitor is there.

Before home care begins, the agency should explain what Medicare is expected to pay and identify services it expects you to pay for, verbally and in writing. This is useful information for planning, not a verdict that every proposed service qualifies. An Advantage enrollee should also confirm the plan’s home health terms. Write the actual ordered visits beside the household’s uncovered hours; keep the medical care plan separate from the family’s assumptions about supervision.

B is the one that sends you a bill every month

Part B is doctors and everything that happens while you’re upright. Medicare.gov’s list: services from doctors and other providers, outpatient care, home health care, durable medical equipment like wheelchairs and walkers, and many preventive services such as screenings, shots and the yearly wellness visit.

Part B costs money every month whether you use it or not. The 2026 standard premium is $202.90 a month, per Medicare.gov, and it can be higher depending on your income, which is a whole chapter of its own later on. The 2026 Part B deductible is $283 a year, once a year, and after you’ve met it you generally pay 20% of the cost of each covered service.

That 20% has no ceiling, and this is the part of Chapter 1 I’d underline if the ink were mine. Medicare.gov says it directly: there’s no yearly limit on what you pay out-of-pocket in Original Medicare unless you have supplemental coverage, like a Medigap policy, or you join a Medicare Advantage plan.

Twenty percent of a knee replacement is not twenty percent of an office visit. Twenty percent of a year with cancer treatment in it is a number nobody can tell you in advance, because the only cap is the one you buy yourself. Remember the second of the two questions from the front of this book, the one about what a bad year could cost you? This is the sentence that makes that question real rather than philosophical.

A few Part B items cost you nothing extra. Medicare.gov lists $0 for covered clinical laboratory services and $0 for covered home health care services, while durable medical equipment runs at the usual 20% of the Medicare-approved amount.

One more thing about those percentages. They assume your doctor accepts the Medicare-approved amount as full payment, which Medicare.gov calls accepting assignment. Most do. Before an expensive procedure with a provider you haven’t used before, it’s a reasonable thing to ask the billing office in plain words.

Ask for the appointment by its covered name

“My annual physical” and “my Medicare wellness visit” sound interchangeable across a reception desk. They are not. Medicare.gov describes the yearly wellness visit as a conversation-based visit to create or update a prevention plan, not a routine physical examination.

The visit includes a health-risk questionnaire, review of medical and family history and current prescriptions, routine measurements, and a written prevention plan. That is useful work. It is not a promise that every test or new health concern raised during the appointment belongs to the same preventive benefit.

The first yearly wellness visit cannot take place within 12 months of Part B enrollment or a Welcome to Medicare preventive visit, the official page says; afterward, the frequency is once every 12 months. The two preventive visits are different benefits. Ask the office which one it is scheduling and whether your previous visit date permits it. A new calendar year alone does not answer a rolling twelve-month question.

In the coverage guidance checked for 2026, the covered wellness visit has no patient charge when the provider accepts assignment, and the Part B deductible does not apply to that preventive benefit. Other tests or services during the appointment may bring deductible or coinsurance charges; something Medicare does not cover, such as a routine physical, may be entirely your responsibility. Ask about those separate services, without withholding symptoms the clinician needs to hear. Medical attention matters more than keeping a visit inside one billing label.

Transport has a similarly important boundary. Part B’s ambulance coverage page requires medical necessity and a situation in which another vehicle could endanger your health. Coverage is to the nearest appropriate facility able to provide the needed care, not automatically to a preferred hospital farther away. Certain non-emergency trips may qualify with the required provider order; being unable to find a ride does not establish ambulance coverage by itself.

For a scheduled non-emergency ambulance trip, ask the ordering clinician and transport company about the coverage conditions and any approval needed. For a medical emergency, get emergency help instead of trying to price the ride first. The coverage question belongs in advance when the trip can safely be planned, not between a frightened person and urgent treatment.

C isn’t a third kind of coverage

Here’s the correction I make most often at that table.

You do not buy Part C in addition to Parts A and B. Medicare Advantage, which is the friendlier name for Part C, is an alternative way to get your Part A and Part B coverage, through a private plan that Medicare has approved. Medicare.gov describes these as bundled plans that include Part A, Part B, and usually Part D.

On the board, then. One, you keep Medicare. Two, a private company administers it for you, under Medicare’s rules. Three, you still pay your Part B premium, and you must keep paying it to stay in the plan, which Medicare.gov states on its cost pages.

What you give and what you get both change inside that arrangement. Medicare.gov says you may need to use doctors in the plan’s network, and get prior authorization for certain drugs or services before you receive them. It also says out-of-pocket costs usually differ from Original Medicare and include a yearly limit on what you pay, and that most plans offer extra benefits Original Medicare doesn’t cover, such as vision, hearing and dental.

A yearly out-of-pocket limit. After a section that just told you Original Medicare has none, you can see why that sentence sells plans. It’s a real advantage, and it isn’t the whole story, and the trade involves networks and permissions rather than only dollars. That comparison is Chapter 3’s entire job, and I’m not going to half-do it here.

The sorting rule for now: Original Medicare plus optional add-ons is one road. A Medicare Advantage plan is the other road. You are not assembling both.

D is drugs, and you pick the plan yourself

Part D helps cover prescription drugs, and Medicare.gov is clear about how you get it: you join a Medicare drug plan alongside Original Medicare, or you get drug coverage by joining a Medicare Advantage plan that includes it. Either way, the plans are run by private insurance companies following rules Medicare sets.

Most people choose and join their own Part D plan, although Medicare automatically enrolls some people who qualify for Extra Help if they do not already have drug coverage. So if you get Extra Help with drug costs, check what plan your name is already sitting in before you shop. Part A and Part B are government coverage with government numbers. Part D is a private plan, from a list that looks identical until you put your own prescriptions into it, and the formulary — the plan’s list of covered drugs — is where the real difference lives. Part D also has a yearly ceiling on what you pay out of pocket for covered drugs, which is a genuinely useful piece of recent design. Chapter 4 does the arithmetic and names the current cap.

The one sentence I want you carrying out of this section: a plan with the lowest premium on the page is not the same thing as the plan that costs you the least this year.

The fifth thing, which isn’t a letter

Medigap belongs in this chapter even though it has no letter of its own, because people confuse it with Part C constantly.

Medigap is extra insurance you buy from a private company to help pay your share of costs in Original Medicare — that uncapped 20%, those repeating deductibles. Medicare.gov says these policies are standardized and, in most states, named by letters like Plan G or Plan K, and that the benefits in each lettered plan are the same no matter which insurance company sells it.

Sit with that last part, because it’s unusual and it’s useful. Two companies selling the same letter in the same state are selling the same benefits. Which means the thing left to compare is price and service, not coverage. Three states run their standardization differently, and I’ll name them in Chapter 5, where Medigap gets the treatment it deserves, including a once-in-a-lifetime window you should know exists before you need it.

Medigap works with Original Medicare. It does not work with a Medicare Advantage plan. That single incompatibility is why Chapter 3’s fork matters more than any other decision in this book.

Which parts do you actually have

Now the practical bit. A surprising number of people don’t know what they’re holding, which makes every further question unanswerable. Take your red, white and blue Medicare card, your plan cards if you have any, and go down this list with a pencil.

  1. Does your Medicare card show HOSPITAL (PART A), and what date does it say coverage started?
  2. Does it show MEDICAL (PART B), with a start date?
  3. Do you have a separate card from a private insurance company that says Medicare Advantage, HMO, PPO or Part C anywhere on it?
  4. If yes to 3, does that same card mention drug coverage, Rx, or Part D?
  5. If no to 3, do you have a separate drug plan card from a private insurer?
  6. Do you have a Medigap or Medicare Supplement policy, and if so, which letter is printed on it?
  7. Is anyone taking a Part B premium out of your Social Security payment, or are you being billed directly?
  8. Write down every drug you take, the dose, and the pharmacy you use. You’ll need this list twice before this book is finished.
  9. Write down every doctor and hospital you refuse to lose. Same reason.

If you answered yes to item 3 and yes to item 6, call the company that sold you the Medigap policy this week. Those two pieces don’t work together, and you may be paying a premium for something that cannot pay a claim.

If item 7 confuses you, or if you’re still working and someone has told you to skip Part B, that’s a question for a professional rather than a book. A licensed agent or a free counselor can see your actual paperwork, which I can’t, and the cost of getting the working-past-65 rules wrong lands on you for years. Chapter 8 lays out the questions to ask them.

What the letters don’t tell you

Four letters, maybe a dozen numbers, and a deductible that can arrive twice in one bad winter. That’s the machinery.

None of it tells you which road to take. That’s still the two questions, and they’re still yours.

The next chapter is the one with a clock in it. Everything in this chapter stays true whether you read it today or in March. The enrollment windows do not wait, and missing one attaches a surcharge to your premium that can follow you for as long as you have the coverage.

Keep the pencil. Go find your card.

Chapter 2: Seven Months, and the Penalty That Doesn’t Expire

Lorraine brings lemon bars to the library on Tuesdays and asks the hardest questions at the table. Two Octobers ago she brought a letter instead.

She wanted me to tell her the number on it was wrong. It wasn’t.

Her husband had died the year she turned 64. His former employer’s retiree plan kept covering her, and it was decent coverage, and so when her birthday came she did the sensible-sounding thing and left it alone. She already had insurance. Why buy Part B on top of it.

Because retiree coverage is not coverage from current work. One word, current, carries that entire distinction, and nobody in any office had said it to her.

Medicare.gov lists this exact situation among the ones that do not qualify for a Special Enrollment Period: your COBRA coverage or retiree coverage ends. So she signed up later, and a late enrollment penalty attached itself to her monthly premium, and it is still there.

She pays more each month than the neighbor who signed up on time, for identical Part B coverage. I told her so in those words, because softening it would only have cost her the chance to plan around it. Then we spent the rest of the hour on what could still be protected.

A clock runs through everything in this chapter. The rules in Chapter 1 hold whether you read them today or next March. These don’t.

The seven months you were given without being told

Your first chance to sign up is called the Initial Enrollment Period. Medicare.gov describes it as lasting seven months, starting three months before the month you turn 65 and ending three months after that month.

Count it out on a calendar rather than in your head. If you turn 65 on June 2 through June 30, your seven months run March through September. If your birthday is June 1, Medicare treats May as your first eligibility month; confirm your exact seven-month window with Social Security’s enrollment calculator before marking it.

Nobody mails you a reminder that your wing is closing.

Now the part almost everyone misses, and it costs real coverage rather than real money. Within those seven months, the date your coverage starts depends on which month you signed up in, and coverage always begins on the first of a month.

Three lines on the board.

  1. If you qualify for premium-free Part A, Medicare.gov says that coverage starts the month you turn 65. If your birthday falls on the first of the month, it starts the month before you turn 65.
  2. For Part B, and for Part A if you have to pay a premium for it, signing up before the month you turn 65 means coverage starts the month you turn 65.
  3. Signing up during the month you turn 65, or in any of the three months after, means coverage starts the following month.

Read line 3 again. If you sign up for Part B in your birthday month, Part B generally starts the next month; it will not cover Part B services before its effective date. Part A may have a different effective date. Check your card and any other coverage before scheduling non-emergency care. Sign up in the third month after instead and that gap is four months long. The window stayed open, you used it, you are not penalized, and the calendar still costs you.

So the instruction is simple and it is the single most useful sentence in this chapter: if you want Medicare coverage in place the month you turn 65, sign up during the three months before your birthday month. Front of the window, not the back.

Premium-free Part A plays by different rules

Part A behaves differently if you qualify for it at no premium, and the difference is generous enough to be worth knowing.

Medicare.gov says you can sign up for premium-free Part A any time after you turn 65. Your Part A coverage then starts six months back from when you sign up or apply for Social Security benefits, though never earlier than the month you turned 65. A retroactive start date, in a program with no other mercies of that kind.

That does not extend to Part B. It does not extend to Part A if you have to buy it. And if you have a Health Savings Account, a retroactive Part A start date can create a problem with the contributions you made during those months, which is a conversation for Chapter 8 where the working-past-65 decisions live.

Part B, once your seven months close, is only available during one of the other enrollment periods. There are three kinds, and they are not interchangeable.

The eight months that depend on one word

If you are 65 or older and still covered by health insurance through your own current job or your spouse’s current job, you may have a Special Enrollment Period instead.

Medicare.gov describes this one carefully, and so will I. It starts the first month after your Initial Enrollment Period ends. It ends eight months after the group health plan coverage ends or the employment ends, whichever happens first. Coverage generally begins the first month after you sign up. And if you sign up while you or your spouse are still working, or within the first full month after the employer coverage ends, you can ask to delay your Part B start date by up to three months.

Four things about that paragraph deserve their own breath.

Whichever happens first. Retire in May with the plan paying claims through August, and your eight months may already be running from May. People lose this window while believing it hasn’t opened yet.

Current. Lorraine’s word. That same Medicare.gov list of disqualifying situations also names COBRA coverage ending, Marketplace coverage, and missing the eight-month window itself. COBRA is the cruelest of those. The envelope arrives looking exactly like a continuation of employer coverage, and for Medicare’s purposes it is not current employment coverage at all.

Disability situations differ. Medicare.gov notes that if you have a disability and your coverage comes from a non-spouse family member’s current employment, that employer must be in a large group health plan for you to be eligible.

End-Stage Renal Disease is carved out. Medicare.gov states that this Special Enrollment Period does not apply if you are eligible for Medicare based on ESRD. If that is your situation, the sequence is different and this is one of the places to call 1-800-MEDICARE rather than trust a general rule.

If you are reading this while still working and someone has told you confidently to skip Part B, stop and verify it against your own employer’s plan documents and your own employer’s size. Not against your brother-in-law, and not against me.

January, March, and the window of last resort

Miss everything above and there is still a door, which Medicare.gov calls the General Enrollment Period: you can sign up between January 1 and March 31 each year, and your coverage starts the month after you sign up. Medicare.gov adds that you might pay a monthly late enrollment penalty if you don’t qualify for a Special Enrollment Period.

Which means a person who realizes in June that they never signed up for Part B is looking at the following January at the earliest, with coverage starting in February or later, and a surcharge riding on top of the premium after that.

That can mean seven months without Part B coverage, followed by a penalty generally charged for as long as you have Part B. Nobody designed that outcome on purpose. It is still the outcome.

One naming problem to clear up while we’re here, because it produces more confusion at my table than any other pair of terms. The General Enrollment Period, January through March, is for people who don’t have Part B yet. The fall window you hear about in television ads, October 15 through December 7, is a different thing entirely, for people who already have Medicare and want to change plans. Chapter 3 handles that one. If somebody tells you in November that you can still sign up for Part B, ask them which window they mean, and then check it yourself.

What a penalty actually does to the number on your bill

Penalties in Medicare are not late fees. Medicare.gov puts it in four blunt lines. They are added to your monthly premium. They are not a one-time late fee. They are usually charged for as long as you have that type of coverage, which for most people means a lifetime penalty. And they go up the longer you wait.

Part B’s arithmetic, per Medicare.gov: you pay an extra 10% for each full 12-month period you could have signed up for Part B and didn’t. Their own worked example uses two full years. Twenty-four months late means a 20% penalty. In 2026 that is $40.58 added to the standard $202.90 premium from Chapter 1, for a monthly premium Medicare.gov calculates at $243.48 and rounds to $243.50. Those are 2026 figures, and both halves of the sum move when the premium moves.

Forty dollars a month does not sound like a catastrophe. Multiply this year’s monthly penalty by 12 for a one-year estimate, then recalculate when the standard premium changes.

Premium-Part A works differently, and this is the one piece of good news in the section. Medicare.gov says that if you have to buy Part A and don’t buy it when you’re first eligible, your monthly premium may go up 10%, and you pay that penalty for twice the number of years you didn’t sign up. Their example: eligible for two years without signing up, so a higher premium for four years. It ends. Part B’s generally does not.

There is a third penalty, attached to Part D, with its own percentage and its own 63-day rule about going without drug coverage. It lives in Chapter 4 alongside the drug plans, because the only sensible way to understand it is next to the thing it applies to.

Medicare.gov also notes that you generally avoid the Part B penalty if you qualify for a Special Enrollment Period or enroll in a Medicare Savings Program, and avoid the Part D penalty if you have creditable drug coverage or qualify for Extra Help. Those last two are Chapter 7, and they are worth looking at even if you assume your income disqualifies you.

That’s the rule. Nobody is asking you to like it.

The windows nobody mentions

The seven months get talked about. What gets far less attention is that Medicare.gov lists a set of other Special Enrollment Periods for Part A and Part B, each with its own clock, several of them created for situations that were plainly unfair before. Here is what Medicare.gov says about each, and the clocks are not the same length.

  1. Lost Medicaid coverage on or after January 1, 2023: the window runs from the date you are notified the coverage is ending through six months after it ends. Coverage starts the first of the month after you sign up, or you can ask for it to start back when the Medicaid coverage ended.
  2. Missed a chance to sign up because of a declared disaster or emergency: the window starts on the day the federal, state, or local government declares it, or on the date stated in the declaration, whichever is earlier. It ends six months after the latest of the original declaration’s end date, the last extension’s end date, or the date the government revokes or announces the end of the incident period. Your coverage starts the first of the next month.
  3. Released from incarceration on or after January 1, 2023: the window runs from the date of release through the twelve months after the month of release. Coverage starts the first of the month after you sign up, or you may request a start as early as the release date, subject to Medicare’s limit of no more than six months of retroactive coverage.
  4. Volunteering in a foreign country: the window starts the first day of the month in which volunteering ends, the organization loses its tax-exempt status, or your qualifying overseas coverage ends, and runs six months from that day. Coverage starts the first of the month after you sign up.
  5. Having TRICARE: the window starts when Social Security notifies you that you missed your chance to enroll and ends twelve months later. Coverage starts the first of the month after you sign up, or you can ask for it to start back to when your Initial Enrollment Period ended.
  6. Inaccurate or misleading information from your health plan or your employer, on or after January 1, 2023: this is the one that matters enormously to anyone in Lorraine’s position going forward. Medicare.gov says the window starts the day you notify the Social Security Administration that your plan or employer misrepresented or gave you incorrect information, and ends six months later.

There is also a Special Enrollment Period for other exceptional conditions, which Medicare.gov says lasts at least six months and requires you to contact Social Security and ask for it. In every one of these, the decision is Social Security’s, not the plan’s and not yours. Ask them for an eligibility decision rather than assuming one.

For several of these, Medicare.gov directs you to form CMS-10797, completed and sent to your local Social Security office by fax or mail.

I am not going to tell you whether your particular story qualifies, because that determination belongs to Social Security and the details matter more than a book can carry. What I will tell you is that if a benefits administrator or an insurance agent told you something in writing that turned out to be wrong, you have a reason to make a phone call rather than a reason to be resigned. Bring the writing. Dates help.

Which window am I in

Take a pencil and answer these in order. Stop at the first one that fits you.

  1. What is your 65th birthday? Write the month and year.
  2. Write the three months before that birthday month, the birthday month, and the three months after. That block is your Initial Enrollment Period. Circle all three months before it: enrolling in any of them puts Part B coverage in place in your birthday month, but do it as early as you can.
  3. Are you 65 or older with coverage based on current employment, yours or your spouse’s? If yes, write the expected end date of both the employment and the coverage. The earlier of those two dates starts your eight-month clock. Do not calculate the final day yourself from this sentence; enter the actual end dates in Medicare’s eligibility tool or have Social Security confirm the last enrollment day in writing.
  4. Is your coverage retiree coverage, COBRA, or a Marketplace plan? Those coverages do not by themselves create the working SEP. Check whether you qualify through current employment or one of Medicare’s other listed special situations before relying on the General Enrollment Period.
  5. Have your seven months already closed with no Part B? Write down next January 1 and next March 31. That is the General Enrollment Period, with coverage starting the month after you sign up.
  6. Did any of these happen to you: lost Medicaid, a declared disaster, release from incarceration, foreign volunteer service, TRICARE, or wrong information from a plan or employer? If yes, call Social Security before you assume you have to wait for January, and ask about form CMS-10797.
  7. Do you have a Health Savings Account you’re still contributing to? Flag it and read Chapter 8 before you sign up for anything, including premium-free Part A.
  8. Have you already enrolled? Find the start date on your card and write it next to item 1, because every later chapter asks you for it.

If items 3 and 4 both seem to describe you, that means somebody has given you conflicting information about your own coverage, and it is exactly the situation to take to a free SHIP counselor or to the employer’s benefits administrator in writing. Ask one question: is this coverage based on current employment, yes or no. Get the answer in an email.

Turn the window into an application

Knowing your enrollment period still leaves a practical question: where does the application go? An Advantage advertisement can put a telephone number directly in front of you without making that number the place to enroll in Part B.

Medicare.gov’s Ready to sign up for Part A and Part B page directs enrollment in those parts to Social Security. Its links differ according to what you already have and why you are applying. Choose your actual situation before opening a form. Buying a private plan is not a substitute for completing the underlying Medicare enrollment.

For a person signing up at 65 for both parts, or only Part A, the page links to Social Security’s online Medicare application. Use that official entry point rather than a sponsored search result. If job-based insurance is ending and you already have Part A, it provides an online route for adding Part B. It also directs the employer to complete CMS-L564, the employment-information form. Submit that evidence to the local SSA office using its postal or fax instructions.

That employer form supplies evidence. It does not itself request every piece of coverage you need. Keep the enrollment application and the employment evidence together so you can tell Social Security what you submitted. If an employer cannot complete its section, Medicare.gov gives an alternative: complete Section B as well as you can without signing it, and provide proof of job-based health insurance. Open the official page’s proof instructions or ask Social Security which records it accepts; do not fabricate an employer signature to finish a packet.

The exceptional-conditions route described earlier uses CMS-10797. Medicare.gov directs that completed application to the local Social Security office. For a Part-A enrollee adding Part B during the General Enrollment Period, its separate instructions name CMS-40B. These form numbers are not interchangeable ways to make the same request. A form downloaded from an old folder may describe a different eligibility route from yours.

For railroad work, the official enrollment page points to the Railroad Retirement Board instead. That is a useful exception to the direction to call Social Security. If you or a spouse worked for a railroad, ask the RRB which office handles your enrollment before sending the packet to an office chosen by habit.

After filing, keep the acknowledgment distinct from the coverage decision. A saved submission screen tells you what you sent; it is not the Medicare card’s effective-date entry. Medicare.gov says the welcome package includes that card and your Medicare Number, which you need for a Medicare account, private-plan enrollment or supplemental coverage. When it arrives, compare the Part A and Part B entries with the start dates you requested and expected.

If they do not agree, take the discrepancy to the enrollment agency promptly. State the application route, submission date and requested start month. Ask what is still needed and what date its record currently shows. This is a concrete follow-up question, unlike “Did I do Medicare right?” Do not cancel existing insurance on the strength of a screen confirming that an application was received; coordinate the actual effective dates with the agency and current insurer.

Three dates on the calendar

Lorraine still comes on Tuesdays. These days she mostly asks questions on behalf of other people, which is its own kind of answer.

Go get a calendar, the paper kind if you have one, and write three things on it. The first of the three months before your 65th birthday month. January 1 of next year. And if you’re working past 65, the date your employment or your employer coverage is expected to end, whichever comes first.

That’s the whole homework. The rules in the next chapter cost money if you choose wrong. These cost money if you simply don’t look.

Chapter 3: Two Roads, and the One Your Doctors Are On

Danny called me from a parking lot in Florida on a Thursday morning in February.

He’d gone to an urgent care the night before with a tightness in his chest. Probably nothing, they told him, but see a cardiologist this week. So that morning he called the office a neighbor had recommended, gave them his information, and got told they weren’t in his plan.

“I have Medicare,” he said. “I’m holding the card.”

He did have Medicare. He also had a Medicare Advantage plan sold in central Pennsylvania, where my brother spends seven months of the year, and a set of Florida doctors he wanted for the other five. Danny believes television. The ad had promised dental, a gym membership, and no monthly premium, and every one of those promises was true, and not one of them was the thing that mattered in that parking lot.

He got seen. It took longer to arrange than a week and cost him more than it would have at home. What it really cost him was a February spent on the phone instead of on a dock.

This is the fork in the road, and the rest of the book arranges itself around it.

Two columns

Original Medicare and Medicare Advantage are two ways of receiving the same underlying coverage, and their trade-offs run in almost exactly opposite directions. That’s why comparing them on one number, any one number, gets people hurt.

Two columns, then.

Left column, Original Medicare. Medicare.gov says you can use any doctor or hospital that takes Medicare, anywhere in the U.S., and the footnote spells out what “anywhere” means: the 50 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, and American Samoa. No plan network. In most cases, Medicare.gov says, you don’t need a referral to see a specialist, and in most cases you don’t need approval in advance for Medicare to cover a service or supply.

Right column, Medicare Advantage. Per Medicare.gov, non-emergency care may have to come from providers inside the plan’s network and service area. Some plans do cover non-emergency care out of network, and it may cost more. A referral may be required to see a specialist. And the plan may require prior authorization before it will cover certain services or supplies.

Now turn to money, where the columns reverse.

Original Medicare’s cost shape you already know from Chapter 1: a monthly Part B premium, usually 20% coinsurance after the deductible, and no yearly ceiling on your share unless you hold supplemental coverage. Medicare.gov names what counts as supplemental: a Medigap policy, or other insurance such as Medicaid, employer, retiree, or union coverage.

A Medicare Advantage plan, per Medicare.gov, has out-of-pocket costs that vary from plan to plan, and a yearly limit on what you pay for covered Medicare services. Reach that limit and you pay nothing for covered services the rest of the year. Read the next part twice: Medicare.gov says that limit may be different for in-network and out-of-network services. One plan, potentially two ceilings, and only one of them applies if you’re seeing someone outside the network.

You keep paying the Part B premium on either road. Medicare.gov adds that with an Advantage plan you may also pay the plan’s own premium, that some plans have a $0 premium, and that some may help pay all or part of your Part B premium.

One last line in each column, and it’s the line nobody learns until they want to move. Medicare.gov says that in Original Medicare you can choose to buy Medigap to help pay the out-of-pocket costs Medicare doesn’t cover. With a Medicare Advantage plan, you can’t buy Medigap to cover your out-of-pocket costs. When you may buy a Medigap policy, and what happens if you try later, is Chapter 5’s whole subject. Do not assume the door you walked through stays propped open behind you.

The third column people forget to draw

Most of what I’ve just described compares an Advantage plan with bare Original Medicare. That comparison is incomplete because supplemental coverage changes Original Medicare’s cost exposure.

So draw the third column: Original Medicare with the Medigap policy introduced in Chapter 1, which per Medicare.gov helps pay the copayments, coinsurance and deductibles Original Medicare leaves to you. Money-wise, that means a monthly premium to the insurer, and Medicare.gov is explicit that your monthly Part B premium continues on top of it, that Medicare pays none of the policy premium, and that such premiums typically increase each year. Medicare.gov also says policies sold after 2005 carry no prescription drug coverage, so a separate Part D plan is usually a third bill.

Which letter covers how much of that cost sharing, and the one-time window to buy without being asked about your health, is Chapter 5’s subject. What matters here is the shape. The Original-plus-Medigap column trades a higher, more predictable monthly bill for less exposure in a bad month. The Advantage column trades a lower monthly bill for a network, a permission step, and a yearly limit you may have to reach the hard way.

You cannot compare the two honestly without a real Medigap number. Medicare.gov lets you compare policy costs in your area, and tells you to contact the insurance company for a more accurate price, because the site’s figures are estimates. Get that quote before you fill in the worksheet at the end of this chapter.

The two words that cost Danny his February

Network and service area.

Danny’s plan did exactly what it was built to do. It covered him well in Cumberland County, where his primary care doctor and the hospital he’d used for twenty years were both in network. Medicare.gov explains that insurance companies decide whether a plan is available to everyone with Medicare in a state or only in certain counties, and that they may offer several plans in one area with different benefits and costs. Plan availability is local, and non-emergency network coverage away from home varies. Danny’s life crossed two service areas.

Which brings me to the question I’d ask before any other. It’s the first one this book opened with, and it isn’t “which plan is best.” It’s this: which doctors, hospitals, and pharmacies do you actually need, and where are they standing?

Where your knees actually get looked at, in other words, rather than where your mail arrives.

A person who sees three specialists at one health system fifteen minutes from the house, and leaves the county twice a year for a wedding, is in a very different position from Danny. For that first person, a plan that includes that health system can work out plainly well. Danny’s current plan did not include that Florida office in its network. He needs to compare the specific plans available where he lives and confirm Florida provider access and out-of-network costs with each plan. Medicare’s own enrollment page says to ask your doctors and pharmacies whether they’re in network with the plan. It also says to check whether the plan will cover you if you live in another state part of the year.

Ask the plan, and then ask the doctor’s billing office separately. Directories go stale, and Medicare.gov puts the question to the providers themselves rather than to a printed list.

While we’re on geography: neither road travels well abroad. Medicare.gov says Original Medicare generally doesn’t cover medical care outside the U.S., though you may be able to buy a Medigap policy that covers emergency care outside the U.S. It says Advantage plans generally don’t cover care outside the U.S. either, and that some plans may offer an extra benefit covering emergency and urgently needed services when you travel. If a cruise or a month in Portugal is in your plans, that’s a question to ask in writing before you enroll, not after.

The initials after the plan name change the answer

An insurer’s name can appear above an HMO and a PPO in the same county. The shared logo does not make the access rules identical. Start with the plan type, then examine the particular product. Medicare.gov has separate official pages for HMOs, PPOs, Private Fee-for-Service plans and Special Needs Plans. Those pages explain differences a slogan about Advantage cannot cover.

An HMO generally directs routine care through its contracted providers. Medicare’s page identifies exceptions for emergency care, out-of-area urgent care and temporary out-of-area dialysis. Some HMO Point-of-Service plans allow specified non-network services with higher cost sharing. The words Point-of-Service do not open every outside office to every service. Have the plan identify what the exception actually covers.

The HMO page also says a primary care doctor is generally required and specialist referrals are required in most cases, with some services excepted. A referral is not the same as authorization: one concerns access through a clinician; the other is a plan’s coverage approval. If a specialist’s office asks for both, obtaining one has not completed the other. Put that distinction beside the appointment you are trying to arrange, rather than memorizing it as another pair of insurance words.

A PPO has a different non-network structure. Its official page allows covered services from outside providers who participate in Medicare or accept assignment, with higher costs possible, and directs you to check coverage and medical necessity with the plan before receiving such care. It says specialist referrals are not required. That does not mean every recommended service bypasses the plan’s authorization conditions or every outside provider agrees to see you.

An outside provider might be eligible under the PPO’s rules but unwilling to accept the appointment; a willing provider might offer a service the plan will not cover under the circumstances proposed. Coverage and appointment availability are separate checks. A label promising non-network access cannot book the visit on your behalf.

Private Fee-for-Service, or PFFS, is another Advantage type, not Original Medicare in a private envelope. Medicare.gov says the provider must accept the plan’s payment terms, agree to treat you, and not have opted out of Medicare. A participating network can give a more settled provider arrangement, but an outside provider may decide at each visit whether to accept those terms. Yesterday’s visit is therefore not sufficient assurance for next month’s planned care.

The PFFS page says no primary care selection or specialist referral is required, and Part A/B-covered services do not require prior approval. Prescription coverage is a separate product check: some PFFS plans include it, while a PFFS plan without it can be paired with a separate drug plan. By contrast, the official HMO and PPO pages say that if you want drug coverage with those types, you must select a version that includes it; you cannot simply add a stand-alone Part D plan to a version without drugs. Have SHIP check an unusual combination before enrollment.

Special Needs Plans, or SNPs, tailor benefits and care coordination to qualifying groups. Medicare.gov identifies dual-eligible, chronic-condition and institutional types. You need Parts A and B, residence in the service area, and the particular plan’s qualifying status. These are HMO or PPO plans, so “special needs” is not a substitute for checking which access model applies. All SNPs provide drug coverage, the official page says.

For a reader with both Medicare and Medicaid, an integrated dual-eligible plan may coordinate the two sets of benefits. That is not an instruction to change your Medicaid arrangement based on this paragraph. Ask the plan and state Medicaid office how the proposed product fits the benefits you actually have. For a chronic-condition plan, ask which condition or group of conditions qualifies; for an institutional plan, verify that its clinicians serve the facility where you live. Availability and eligibility are local questions with individual answers.

One approval protection deserves attention before a change during treatment. Medicare.gov describes a transition safeguard on its HMO and PPO pages: the new plan must allow at least 90 days before asking for new prior approval of ongoing treatment. Those pages also describe approval lasting while the authorized treatment remains medically necessary. This does not establish that an old clinician is in the new network or that all bills will match the old plan’s terms.

For planned enrollment during a course of care, have the new plan explain how it will handle that specific course and have the treating office check the arrangement. Give them the treatment and relevant approval, not just the diagnosis. The useful answer identifies what continues, who provides it, and any remaining coverage conditions. Do this before a safe, planned switch; a continuity provision should prevent an interruption, not become a vague reassurance after one occurs.

What the extra benefits are and aren’t

The dental and the gym membership are real, and I won’t pretend otherwise to make a point.

Medicare.gov says Original Medicare covers most medically necessary services and supplies in hospitals, doctors’ offices, and other health care facilities, and that it doesn’t cover some services, including routine physical exams, eye exams, and most dental care. It says Advantage plans must cover all medically necessary services that Original Medicare covers, and may also offer extra benefits Original Medicare doesn’t, like some vision, hearing, and dental services.

Note the word some, which Medicare.gov uses and which the television ad does not. A dental benefit carries its own limit and its own list of what’s included, and that limit lives in the plan’s own documents rather than in any federal rule I can quote you.

So price the extras honestly. A cleaning twice a year is worth real money. A cardiologist in the month you need him is worth more. If both columns genuinely work for your doctors, then extras are a sensible tiebreaker and I’d use them that way.

Prior authorization lands on your calendar

Prior authorization is easy to underestimate because it sounds administrative.

Medicare.gov says an Advantage plan may require its approval first, and that Original Medicare, in most cases, does not. What that buys you is a third party standing between a doctor’s recommendation and the calendar, and sometimes that party says no, and then you’re appealing instead of healing.

Advantage plans can fit readers whose providers are in network and who value a medical out-of-pocket limit. The trade is a network and, for some services, prior authorization. For some readers, an Advantage plan’s yearly out-of-pocket limit is a genuine protection that Original Medicare alone does not provide. It is a yearly ceiling on your cost-sharing for covered Medicare services, while premiums, drug costs, and non-covered care still require separate budgeting. Anybody who describes that trade as one-sided is selling something.

The usual advice here annoys me in both of its flavors. “Advantage plans are a trap” ignores people for whom a hard dollar ceiling is the difference between sleeping and not. “Original Medicare is for people who don’t do math” ignores Danny in a parking lot. Neither slogan has met your doctor list.

When the plan says no

A denial letter can sit beside a bill and make both harder to read. Separate them first. An ordinary deductible or coinsurance charge may be correct; a refusal to cover care, pay a claim, or change a disputed amount is a decision you can challenge. Medicare.gov’s Filing an appeal page describes those rights. A grievance concerns service or care quality rather than that coverage decision. If you cannot identify what happened, ask the decision-maker which process fits before sending anything.

Use this decision tree to find the right door:

  1. Covered care is about to end: Read the hospital’s “An Important Message from Medicare about Your Rights” or the other provider’s “Notice of Medicare Non-Coverage.” Follow its BFCC-QIO instructions for independent fast review. Medicare.gov’s fast-appeals page gives the hospital deadline as the planned discharge day; for skilled nursing, home health, comprehensive outpatient rehabilitation and hospice, it gives noon on the day before the listed termination date. Ask for a missing notice immediately. Medicare Advantage also has plan appeal routes with different rules; do not substitute a plan’s ordinary process for the fast-review instructions on your service-ending notice.
  2. Original Medicare decided a claim: Start with the Medicare Summary Notice’s appeal instructions. The first level is a redetermination. Use the claim information, destination and deadline printed there rather than sending it to a private insurer that happens to cover another part of your care.
  3. An Advantage plan denied medical coverage or payment: Request the plan’s review using its written decision. Its first review and later independent review are part of the health-plan appeal route. If waiting could seriously harm your health, involve the treating clinician and ask about expedited review. That urgency request is distinct from a hospital discharge appeal.
  4. A drug plan denied a medicine: Use that plan’s written drug-decision instructions. If no coverage decision exists yet, a coverage determination or exception request may be the first step; Chapter 4 explains the restrictions a prescriber may need to address. An appeal challenges a decision already made, not merely an unfavorable shopping estimate.

Across these routes, Medicare.gov describes generally five review levels. Each decision letter explains whether and how you can continue. You need the next permitted step, not five forms completed at once. If a filing date has passed, ask the decision-maker whether a late request can be considered and what evidence it requires; do not assume extra time is available.

The following checklist is the whole notice-and-submission job. Use it once for the decision in front of you:

  • Identify the member, service or medicine, date, claim or decision number, and the exact reason given. Read the full notice, including its final instructions page.
  • Copy its filing deadline and accepted submission method. Name the person who will file; a provider’s offer to help does not establish that it has submitted anything.
  • Ask the provider for the evidence that answers the stated reason: an order, missing record, factual correction, or clinical explanation. Keep unrelated paperwork out of the packet.
  • State what you want reconsidered, using the required form or portal. List attachments so the reviewer can connect each document to the disputed decision.
  • Retain the submitted copy and transmission confirmation, then check receipt without letting that call replace timely filing. Save the next determination with its new instructions.
  • If someone acts for you, ask Medicare or the plan what representative authorization is required. Use its approved channel for private medical information.

Suppose, as a worked example, an Advantage notice refuses an outpatient therapy request because the file lacks the clinician’s explanation of why skilled therapy is needed. This is an invented paperwork situation, not an account of a successful appeal. The response should address the missing explanation, not argue that all therapy must be covered.

The reader gives the clinician the actual notice. The office can identify the requested treatment and explain the relevant medical facts. The appeal’s short opening asks for reconsideration of that named service and points to the dated clinical statement. The reader submits through the notice’s specified route, keeps confirmation, and reads the resulting decision. If the denial actually cites a different reason, this example’s response is the wrong one. Evidence must fit the letter you received.

That is enough structure to begin without inventing an insurance argument. SHIP offers free help reading Medicare appeal documents. When the dispute puts essential treatment or substantial costs at stake, seek prompt assistance from the treating provider and, if legal questions require it, a qualified attorney. A counselor cannot extend a deadline by taking the letter home. An appeal does not promise payment or tell you to stop treatment; urgent medical decisions belong with the clinician, and immediate danger calls for emergency care rather than an insurance queue.

Last year’s plan was last year’s plan

Here’s the part that catches people who did everything right once.

Medicare.gov states that each year, insurance companies can decide to join or leave Medicare. It says that if a plan decides to stop participating in Medicare, you’ll have to join another Medicare health plan or return to Original Medicare. It lists reasons a plan can disenroll you, including moving outside the plan’s service area, and says those situations come with a grace period and a Special Enrollment Period.

So the plan can change its network. It can change what it charges and what it covers. It can leave your county. The decision you made last fall was a decision about last year’s plan, and the plan you’re in next January is a different document with the same name on the envelope.

That’s why Medicare is an annual chore rather than a one-time choice, and why the fall window exists at all.

The two windows that let you move

Chapter 2 drew the line between the January-through-March General Enrollment Period, for people who haven’t got Part B yet, and the fall window everyone hears about on television. Here is that fall window, and its lesser-known cousin.

Medicare’s Open Enrollment Period runs October 15 through December 7. Per Medicare.gov, during those weeks you can join, drop, or switch Medicare Advantage plans, with or without drug coverage. You can switch from Original Medicare to an Advantage plan, or from an Advantage plan back to Original Medicare. And if you’re in Original Medicare, you can join, drop, or switch a Medicare drug plan. Coverage starts January 1 of the next year, and the plan must receive your request by December 7.

The deadline is December 7, not New Year’s Eve. Write it on the calendar in the kitchen.

Then there’s the Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period, January 1 through March 31, and Medicare.gov is specific that it’s only for people already in an Advantage plan. During it you can switch to a different Advantage plan, with or without drug coverage. Or you can drop the Advantage plan and return to Original Medicare, which also lets you join a separate Medicare drug plan. The new coverage begins on the first day of the month after your request reaches the plan.

There’s a related door for people brand new to all of this. If you joined a Medicare Advantage plan during your Initial Enrollment Period, Medicare.gov says you may switch Advantage plans or return to Original Medicare during the first three months you have both Part A and Part B. During the January 1-March 31 Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period, a person already in an Advantage plan may make only one change.

So a person who enrolls in an Advantage plan at 65, uses it in the first weeks, and discovers what Danny discovered, has a door. One door, once, early on. Whether a Medigap policy is still available to that person on the same terms is a separate question with its own rules. That’s Chapter 5, and it’s why I’d rather you get this right in the fall than fix it in the spring.

One more thing before the worksheet, and it’s the place to stop reading and make a phone call. If you have health coverage now through an employer or a union, yours or a spouse’s, Medicare.gov says to ask that benefits administrator about their rules before you join a Medicare Advantage plan. Joining one might, in some cases, cost you the employer or union coverage. Medicare.gov adds that if you drop or lose it for yourself, your spouse and dependents may lose it too, and you may not get it back. That is not a risk to evaluate from a book. Put the question to your benefits administrator in writing, and bring the answer to a free SHIP counselor before you enroll in anything.

Where do you actually spend the year

Five questions. Write the answers down, because the last two are the ones that change people’s minds.

  1. List every doctor, specialist, hospital, and pharmacy you used in the last two years, and write the city next to each. Add anyone you expect to need: an orthopedist for the knee, the oncologist you still see once a year. If the list spans two states or two health systems, say so at the top of the page in capital letters.
  2. Count the months. How many nights did you sleep somewhere other than your own house last year, and where? A month with a daughter in Oregon is not a vacation as far as a network is concerned. Write the months and the places.
  3. For each plan you’re considering, check every name on your list two ways: in the plan’s directory, and by calling the provider’s billing office to ask whether they’re in network with that specific plan for the coming year. Write the date of the call and the name of the person who answered. Then ask Medicare’s Plan Finder at Medicare.gov whether the plan serves your county.
  4. Finish this sentence on paper: in a bad year, I could pay out of pocket up to ______ before it damages us. That household limit is the number everything else gets measured against, and it’s the one people answer last and feel first.
  5. Build a same-use scenario, not a worst-case ranking. Choose one plausible medical year, such as an inpatient admission followed by six specialist visits and a course of outpatient therapy, with the same services, settings and prescriptions for every option. Ask the providers and each insurer to price those assumptions for the coverage year. Keep annual premiums on their own line: Part B, then the Advantage premium or the Medigap and separate Part D premiums. On a second line, enter estimated cost sharing for the scenario’s covered medical services, after any supplement pays. On a third, enter the drug-only estimate for that same prescription list and pharmacy; do not add premiums or deductibles twice. On a fourth, price the same uncovered-care assumptions, such as dental work, using actual quotes. Record each Advantage plan’s in-network limit and any out-of-network or combined limit separately as protections, not predicted bills. Ask which limit applies to the providers in this scenario and which expenses count toward it. For Medigap, price the medical share left by that specific policy version; for bare Original Medicare, note that the estimate has no annual medical ceiling. Write “cannot estimate” beside any unpriced service or uncertain coverage rather than treating it as zero. Add only the priced components, label the total incomplete if anything is missing, and ask SHIP to check this comparison before a coverage switch.

If question 1 names two states, or question 5 produces a total above the number in question 4, you have a real conflict rather than a simple preference, and that’s exactly the conversation to take to a SHIP counselor, who is free and sells nothing. Medicare.gov keeps the directory at shiphelp.org and lists the agent and broker marketing rules on its own site, which is worth a look before you take anybody’s call.

Danny’s second winter

Danny and I spent an evening at my kitchen table the following October with his list, his two states, and a legal pad. He made a different choice for the next year, and I’m deliberately not telling you which one, because his list isn’t yours and that’s the entire point of this chapter.

Go write your list. Doctors, cities, months. One page, in pencil.

Chapter 4 takes the same honest-arithmetic approach to the drugs you pick up at the counter, where the sticker premium misleads even more reliably than it does here.

Chapter 4: The Premium Is Not the Price

Joan had a pharmacy printout folded in half on our kitchen table. She read the names off it while I entered them into Medicare’s Plan Finder: one at a time, with the strength and the number of pills. Then we did it again with the pharmacy we actually used.

The plan with the lowest monthly premium looked like the bargain until the yearly estimates were on the screen. For our list and that pharmacy, another plan came out lower over the year. We hadn’t found a trick. We’d finally compared the thing we were going to pay, not just the first number on the page.

That distinction matters more with prescriptions than almost anywhere else in Medicare. Two plans can both offer Part D and still cover different drugs, price the same drug differently, or use different pharmacies for their best rates. A plan name is not a promise about the bottle you pick up.

A list of medicines is not a list of plan prices

Medicare.gov explains that each Medicare drug plan sets its own premium, deductible, copayments or coinsurance, and list of covered drugs, within Medicare’s rules. Drug coverage can come from a stand-alone Part D plan or from a Medicare Advantage plan that includes drug coverage. If you have employer, union, or other health benefits, ask the benefits administrator how a change would affect them before you switch anything.

The list of covered drugs is called a formulary. It is specific to the plan and coverage year. One plan may cover the drug you take; another may not. A covered drug can also land in a different cost tier, and the plan may set conditions for coverage. Read the current formulary and the plan’s Evidence of Coverage, not last year’s printout or a search result with a familiar insurer’s name on it.

Check the details against the prescription as it is written: exact drug name, strength, form, and usual quantity. A tablet and a liquid with the same medicine are not interchangeable entries in a price estimate. If your prescription has a generic option, enter the medicine you actually take first. You can ask your prescriber whether an alternative is appropriate, but don’t substitute one on your own to make a plan comparison look better.

The pharmacy matters, too. A plan can have preferred pharmacies, standard network pharmacies, and pharmacies outside its network. The price shown can change depending on which one you choose. Mail order may be an option, but do not assume it is cheaper or suits every prescription. Check the pharmacy you would really use, and check another nearby option only if you would actually go there.

Three restrictions that are not prices

A formulary entry can show a medicine as covered and still leave work to do before the pharmacy can fill it under the plan. Medicare.gov’s Drug plan rules page distinguishes prior authorization, step therapy and quantity limits. Treat those entries as conditions to investigate, not decorations beside a reassuring price.

Prior authorization requires approval under the plan’s conditions. The prescriber may need to establish medical necessity or show that the drug is being used for a condition the plan covers. A prescription order and an authorization approval are different documents. The doctor can intend a medicine for you without the plan having received the information it requires to cover that use.

For shopping purposes, the question is whether your current prescription meets that plan’s conditions and what must be submitted if it does not. Ask the prescriber’s office to evaluate the clinical requirements, not to promise that a familiar diagnosis will automatically satisfy them. A plan’s previous approval under an old product or coverage year should not silently become the assumption behind a new plan estimate.

Step therapy requires trying a specified drug before coverage of another drug under the rule. Medicare.gov explains that an exception can be requested when the prescriber considers the requested medicine necessary, the alternative likely to cause adverse effects, or the alternative less effective.
