The prescriber supplies the medical explanation. The reader’s preference for a bottle is not the same thing as that supporting statement.

If you already tried the proposed first-step drug, tell the prescriber and identify the relevant treatment record. Do not try it again on your own to make the paperwork look tidy. If you have not tried it, the clinical question is whether it is appropriate for you, not whether a plan worksheet becomes cheaper after you type in its name. This book cannot decide that treatment question, and a drug comparison should not decide it accidentally.

A quantity limit concerns the amount covered within a period. The official page uses a plan covering 30 tablets per month as an example, not a limit applying to every prescription. Compare the restriction with the actual directions on your label. One tablet twice a day does not fit the same monthly quantity as one tablet daily. Entering only the drug’s name can conceal that difference from the person reviewing your shopping sheet.

The prescriber may request a quantity exception when the plan’s limit is not medically appropriate for the patient. That is different from asking a pharmacy to split a fill without knowing how the plan will process it. Put the prescribed amount and the stated limit side by side, then let the plan and prescriber establish the route. Do not stretch doses or ration a medicine while waiting for a price question to be resolved.

These three restrictions can make two identical-looking formulary prices different practical choices. The lower estimate may depend on a rule you have not yet satisfied. On the worksheet, mark that cost conditional until the required coverage question is answered. A verified restriction is more useful than a favorable total built on an untested assumption.

An exception is a clinical request, not a shopping discount

Medicare.gov’s How do drug plans work? page describes formulary exceptions and tiering exceptions. The first can seek coverage for a drug absent from the list or waiver of a rule. The second can seek a lower cost-sharing level for a medicine on a non-preferred tier. The terms matter because they ask for different changes.

The prescriber must provide a supporting medical statement. Ask the plan what request is available for the particular medicine and situation; do not assume that every specialty drug can simply be moved to the cheapest tier. If you are comparing plans before enrollment, an exception you hope to obtain is not existing coverage. Keep the advertised benefit and the requested departure from it on separate lines.

A useful shopping note might say that the medicine is absent and the prescriber is reviewing an exception request. That note identifies uncertainty without predicting its outcome. It would be misleading to enter the price of a listed alternative while continuing to assume you will receive the original drug. Compare what is actually covered and flag what remains undecided.

Plans can change their formularies during the year under Medicare’s guidelines, the official page explains, and must notify you of changes affecting medicines you take. It also notes that coinsurance can rise when the manufacturer’s price rises. Fixed copayments and percentage-based coinsurance do not respond identically to a changing price. Read a notice about the particular medicine when it arrives rather than treating last fall’s estimate as a contract for every later refill.

If an exception or coverage request is denied, use Chapter 3’s appeal tree rather than starting a second procedure from these shopping notes. The denial’s instructions determine the next step. Before a denial, the job here is narrower: identify the restriction, have the prescriber assess it, and ask the plan for the correct coverage request.

The first fill may arrive before the card

There is a practical gap between joining a plan and holding its plastic card. Medicare.gov’s Using your drug coverage page explains what to show the pharmacy if the new card has not arrived: the plan’s acknowledgment or welcome letter, or its enrollment confirmation number together with the plan name and phone number. An official printable Medicare card may also help the pharmacy locate the coverage record.

Keep the plan’s effective date with those items. Evidence that an application was received does not authorize you to treat future coverage as active today. Ask the plan and pharmacy to confirm the coverage they are using for the fill, especially near a changeover. A rejection caused by missing membership information is not necessarily a clinical denial of the medicine.

Bring photo identification and the drug-plan card when available, plus the Medicare card. For someone with Medicaid or Extra Help, the official page says to bring proof of that assistance too, so the pharmacy can apply the correct drug charges. Chapter 7 handles eligibility and applications; at the counter, this is about showing the benefit already awarded.

If the pharmacy cannot locate the plan information and you pay yourself, save the detailed receipt and contact the plan. Medicare.gov says some spending may be reimbursed or credited toward eligible out-of-pocket costs. It does not promise that every cash purchase will be refunded. Ask which claim process applies before assuming the amount belongs in the covered-drug estimate.

When new drug coverage begins, Medicare.gov’s rules page says you may receive a one-time transition fill of a medicine you already take that is absent from the formulary or subject to prior authorization or step therapy. It describes a 30-day supply and tells you to check the particular plan’s rules. That possible bridge is not permanent coverage and is not a reason to ignore a restriction during enrollment.

Ask what happens before the next fill is due. The prescriber may need to request an exception, complete authorization, or discuss a clinically suitable change. A temporary supply gives time for that work if it applies; it does not settle it. Keep treatment decisions with the prescriber, especially when an interruption could be harmful.

A pharmacy receipt may belong to a different part

Part D does not own every medicine used by a person with Medicare. The official drug-plan explanation says Part A generally covers drugs supplied as part of treatment during a covered inpatient hospital or skilled nursing stay. Part B covers a limited set of outpatient drugs under its conditions, including some administered in a clinician’s office. The place and method of administration can change the coverage question.

Insulin supplies a concrete example without adding another price chart. Medicare.gov’s insulin page assigns insulin used in a pump covered under Part B’s durable-equipment benefit to Part B. Injectable insulin and insulin used with some other pumps may be covered through Part D. Do not change equipment or delivery method for a plan estimate. Ask the treating team and plan which benefit applies to the actual product and device you use.

That distinction matters to a yearly worksheet. A drug paid through a medical benefit should not quietly be priced as a Part D prescription and then counted toward the Part D cap. Keep any medical-benefit drug expense with the appropriate medical estimate. The drug’s familiar name does not establish which program pays the particular claim.

Hospital outpatient care creates another awkward boundary. Medicare.gov explains that Part B generally does not cover the self-administered medicines you would normally take yourself while in an emergency department or observation setting. Part D may cover them under certain circumstances, with payment first and a reimbursement claim afterward. Ask the hospital for an itemized drug charge and the drug plan how it handles that claim. Do not assume that a hospital wristband places the whole medicine bill under Part A.

Vaccines also divide between benefits. The official drug-plan page names COVID-19, flu, hepatitis B and pneumococcal vaccines among those covered by Part B, while Part D covers other medically necessary commercially available vaccines under its rules. Its guidance checked in 2026 says adult vaccines recommended by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices have no out-of-pocket charge under Part D. Ask the vaccinating provider which benefit it will bill and whether the service meets the coverage conditions; do not predict a charge merely from the word “shot.”

For a planned service, that benefit check can happen before the appointment. It is not a medical recommendation to get or skip a vaccine. The clinician supplies that advice. The coverage question is which card, provider arrangement and program rules apply to the service recommended for you.

Price the pharmacy you can reach

The official pharmacy page distinguishes preferred contracted pharmacies from other contracted locations. A preferred pharmacy may charge less than another pharmacy in the same network. “In network” therefore answers a coverage-access question without necessarily identifying the lowest cost.

Mail order can provide up to a three-month supply for some covered medicines, Medicare.gov says. Before counting its estimate, consider whether you can use that arrangement for the prescription and where deliveries would go. Ask about the plan’s actual mail-order terms and refill service, rather than assuming every medicine can be supplied that way. A hypothetical saving at a pharmacy you will not use is not a household saving.

For an outside-network purchase, the official page warns that you may have to pay the full price. It says to retain receipts and ask the plan whether part can be refunded, with out-of-network cost sharing not refundable. Contact the plan about its conditions. Do not carry the preferred-pharmacy estimate onto a receipt from somewhere else and expect the two amounts to match.

When comparing a nearby pharmacy with mail order, hold the drug, quantity and coverage year constant. If the quantities differ, identify that difference before attributing the whole price gap to the pharmacy. This is a test of the comparison’s inputs, not another instruction to choose the lowest visible number.

The number to compare is the whole year

The monthly premium is real. It is also only one line. Medicare.gov’s drug-cost page lists premiums, deductibles, copayments and coinsurance as possible costs; the amounts depend on the plan. Use the same prescriptions, quantities and pharmacy for every plan you compare, then inspect the Plan Finder’s cost breakdown so you know which pieces its annual estimate includes.

Here is the arithmetic to put on paper:

  1. Write the monthly premium for the plan year, then multiply it by 12. If the plan has a separate income-related charge, keep that separate; Chapter 6 covers that subject.
  2. Add the Plan Finder’s estimated yearly spending for your prescriptions, using its breakdown to identify projected cost-sharing. If the displayed annual total already includes the plan premium, do not add that premium again; if it separates premium and drug spending, combine those lines. Do not add the deductible a second time when it is already reflected in the estimate.
  3. Add costs the estimate does not cover, such as a medicine the plan excludes or a purchase you expect to make outside the plan. Ask the plan how that purchase is treated before counting it as covered spending.
  4. Write the plan name, coverage year, pharmacy, date you checked, and any assumptions beside the total. Keep the worksheet with the formulary and plan documents you used.

The result is an estimate, not a bill. Your prescriptions can change; the plan’s rules can affect when a medicine is covered; and a doctor may prescribe something new midyear. But using one list consistently is a much better comparison than setting a premium from one plan beside a premium from another and calling the smaller one a winner.

If a plan’s estimate surprises you, look for the item causing the difference. Is the drug not on the formulary? Is it in a higher tier? Did you select a different pharmacy or quantity? Did the estimate include a deductible? Check the plan’s own current documents, then call the plan if the answer remains unclear. Write down the date and the name or reference number for the call.

The cap has a year attached to it

Part D also has an annual out-of-pocket limit for covered drugs. This is not a ceiling on everything you spend for health care, and it is not a ceiling on every dollar you spend at a pharmacy. The plan premium is separate. A drug that is not covered may not count toward the limit. Medicare.gov’s cost page explains which eligible spending counts, including certain payments made on your behalf, such as Extra Help.

The current figure is not the figure printed last year. Medicare.gov’s Part D cost page lists a $2,100 out-of-pocket limit for 2026 and a $2,400 limit for 2027. It also lists the maximum plan deductible as $615 in 2026 and $700 in 2027; some plans set a lower deductible or none at all. Those are year-specific federal limits, not a forecast of what any one person’s plan will cost. The plan’s own premium, formulary and cost-sharing still matter.

After your counted spending on covered Part D drugs reaches the limit for that coverage year, Medicare.gov says you automatically enter catastrophic coverage and pay nothing out of pocket for covered Part D drugs for the rest of that year. The phrase covered Part D drugs is doing important work. A premium remains a premium. A drug the plan does not cover is a different problem, and a medical service is not part of this drug limit.

Medicare.gov’s figures can change as the program’s annual amounts are set. As I write on October 4, 2026, its page gives both the 2026 and 2027 Part D amounts. Before making a decision, confirm the number for the year your coverage starts at Medicare.gov’s Medicare drug coverage cost page. If a later official update changes a figure, use the new official figure, not this paragraph.

The cap is useful for a particular kind of bad year: one with substantial covered prescription costs. It cannot tell you which plan covers your medicines or whether you can use your pharmacy. Nor does the cap make every Part D plan cost the same. Your comparison still begins with the list in your hand.

The penalty follows a gap, not a bad shopping choice

Missing Part D when you first become eligible can have a longer tail than one enrollment season. Medicare.gov says you may owe a late enrollment penalty if, after your Initial Enrollment Period, you go 63 or more days in a row without Part D or other creditable prescription drug coverage. Creditable means coverage expected to pay, on average, at least as much as standard Medicare drug coverage.

The penalty is generally based on the number of full uncovered months and the national base beneficiary premium for the relevant year. Medicare.gov describes the calculation as 1% of that base amount for each uncovered month, rounded to the nearest ten cents and added to your Part D premium. The base amount can change. I am not putting a 2027 penalty dollar figure here; check Medicare.gov’s current penalty calculation for the year it applies to you.

The additional amount normally stays attached to Part D each month you remain enrolled, including after a plan switch. Medicare.gov says people who qualify for Extra Help do not pay it while receiving that help. The plan tells you whether it has assessed a penalty when you join. If the notice does not match your coverage history, ask the plan how it counted the months and contact Medicare or a SHIP counselor for help reviewing the decision.

Do not decide that another policy is creditable just because it pays for prescriptions. Medicare.gov advises people to look for a notice from their employer or other coverage provider stating whether the drug coverage is creditable. If you are not sure, ask that provider in writing before you drop the coverage. This is especially important for people with retiree, union, VA, or other coordinated benefits; one change can affect benefits beyond the drug plan itself.

Use Plan Finder as a calculator, then verify the result

Medicare’s Plan Finder is built for the comparison Joan and I needed. Medicare.gov now lets people review 2027 plan options. For each plan, enter your ZIP code, the year you need, every prescription, the correct dose and quantity, and each pharmacy you are genuinely willing to use. If you have a Medicare account, the site may let you use saved drugs and pharmacies; still check that the saved list is current.

Then compare the plans on the same terms. Start with the yearly drug-cost estimate, not the monthly premium column. Look at the premium and deductible as well, so you understand why the estimate differs. Check the coverage details for every medicine that matters to you and check each pharmacy. Save or print the results with the date. A result without its year and assumptions is a scrap of paper with a short memory.

Plan Finder gives an estimate, not an exact pharmacy charge or a promise that your prescriptions will stay the same. Before enrolling, review the plan’s current formulary and Evidence of Coverage. If one important medicine is absent or has a restriction you cannot work around, call the plan and ask what options it offers. Your prescriber can discuss clinically suitable alternatives. If you are about to run out of an essential medicine or believe a coverage decision is wrong, contact the prescriber and the plan promptly rather than waiting for the next enrollment season.

If you need help with the comparison, a SHIP counselor can walk through the choices without selling you a plan. Medicare.gov also lists 1-800-MEDICARE. A licensed insurance agent may explain plan terms, but ask who the agent represents and how they are paid; do not let a sales call replace checking the plan’s own documents. If you have complex employer or retiree benefits, talk with that benefits administrator before enrolling or disenrolling.

A worksheet that fits beside the pharmacy printout

Use one copy for each plan. Keep the coverage year the same on every page.

  1. Plan name and coverage year: ______________________________
  2. Monthly premium: __________ x 12 = annual premium: __________
  3. Pharmacy selected in Plan Finder: ___________________________
  4. Prescriptions entered, including strength and quantity: ______
  5. Plan Finder’s estimated annual drug spending: _______________
  6. Does that estimate include the annual premium? Yes / No / unclear
  7. Important coverage conditions or excluded drugs to verify: ____
  8. Likely purchases not included in the covered-drug estimate: ___
  9. Estimated annual total, with assumptions written beside it: ___
  10. Date checked and plan contact, if you called: _______________

Do not write the annual deductible again as an extra cost if the Plan Finder estimate already includes what you would pay toward it. The deductible is part of the route through the estimate, not automatically a second bill on top of the estimate. If you cannot tell what the total includes, ask the plan or Medicare before relying on your arithmetic.

If income-related Part D charges may apply, keep them on a separate line and use the current figure for the year in question; Chapter 6 explains the lookback and appeal route. If you may qualify for Extra Help, check before ruling it out. Chapter 7 covers where to apply and how it changes drug costs.

Joan still keeps that pharmacy list in the kitchen drawer. The useful part is not the drawer. It’s that the list has the names, strengths and quantities, so we don’t have to start from memory every fall.

Before you compare plans, make your own list from the labels or your pharmacy’s current printout. Put the strength next to each name. Then take that page to Medicare.gov and price the year, not the advertisement.

Chapter 5: Six Months That Don’t Come Back Every Fall

The application is open on a laptop, waiting at a question about hospital stays. The applicant has had Part B for several years. Now they want Medigap, and the company wants a medical history before deciding whether to sell it.

This is an illustration, not somebody else’s claim file. Suppose the applicant left Original Medicare’s unpaid share to savings at first, then decided to buy a policy after treatment made that share harder to manage. Outside a protected buying window, an insurer may use medical underwriting. The application can end with a higher price, fewer choices, or a refusal.

Nothing about being allowed to return to Original Medicare answers that application question. Chapter 3 gave you the switching calendar. Medigap has its own calendar, and a right to make one change does not establish a right to buy the other coverage.

I’d rather you meet that distinction here, with no application pending.

What happens to the unpaid share

Medicare.gov’s Medigap pages describe a policy that helps pay your portion of covered Original Medicare bills. You generally need both A and B to buy it. Medicare pays first. The supplement pays according to its benefits, and whatever remains is yours.

It addresses specified deductibles, copayments and coinsurance. Depending on the letter, an item may be paid completely, paid partly or left to you.

Medicare.gov says Medigap generally excludes long-term care, vision and dental care, hearing aids, glasses and private-duty nursing. If you’re imagining help bathing and dressing in a nursing home, don’t mistake a supplement’s skilled-nursing coinsurance benefit for insurance against that long-term expense. They answer different bills.

Some policies include foreign travel emergency benefits, within limits. Read the conditions before relying on one abroad.

For prescriptions, keep the comparison from Chapter 4; a newly purchased Medigap policy does not add drug coverage. And the supplement belongs on the Original Medicare side of Chapter 3’s comparison. Medicare.gov says it cannot pay an Advantage plan’s premiums or cost sharing. If you’re arranging a return to Original Medicare, confirm that transition separately from the supplement application.

A Medigap policy covers one person, according to Medicare.gov. A couple needs separate policies if both want it, with each person’s eligibility, premium and effective date on their own paperwork.

The letter is the benefits, not the company’s name

In most states the standardized choices are Plans A, B, C, D, F, G, K, L, M and N. These are Medigap plan names. Plan B is not Medicare Part B; Plan D is not prescription coverage. Somebody allowed both alphabets into the same room, and the rest of us have to label our papers carefully.

According to Medicare.gov’s basics page, companies selling the same letter sell the same standardized basic benefits. For that coverage comparison, price is the difference between insurers. Paying more for a standard Plan G does not turn it into a richer standard Plan G.

Choose the benefits first. Comparing prices for different letters can make less coverage look like a discount on the same thing.

There are qualifications. Medicare.gov lists high-deductible versions of Plans F and G in some states. A high-deductible G and a standard G do not start paying at the same point. Write out the version, not just the letter, and check the current figure for the high deductible on Medicare.gov’s comparison page.

Medicare SELECT is another qualification. Medicare.gov says these policies may require particular providers and may have a lower premium. Ask whether a quote is for SELECT before treating it as interchangeable with a standard policy. Chapter 3’s provider list still has work to do here.

Medicare.gov explains that Plans C and F are unavailable to people newly eligible for Medicare on or after January 1, 2020. Earlier eligibility can change that answer, including for someone who had Medicare before 65. First eligibility controls, not the day you decided to shop. Ask Medicare or SHIP if your history makes the cutoff unclear.

The letter chart is not an alphabetical ranking. Read the benefits you would buy.

Read down the chart, not across an advertisement

Open Medicare.gov’s Compare Medigap Plan Benefits page. It shows each benefit as a separate row. A full-coverage mark applies to that named benefit; it does not mean the policy covers every medical expense.

Start with the Part A deductible and hospital cost sharing from Chapter 1, then skilled nursing facility coinsurance. Ask what the candidate pays in each row. A “No” means that policy leaves that row’s cost with you, however generous the rows above look.

Next examine Part B. Standard Plan G leaves its annual deductible to you while covering the coinsurance and excess-charge benefits shown in the federal chart. That describes bills after the deductible, without promising payment for excluded services.

Plan N has a different shape. Medicare.gov’s chart identifies copayments for some office visits and emergency department visits when you aren’t admitted as an inpatient. It does not cover the Part B deductible or the excess-charge row. Read the current copayment amounts on the official page and ask the insurer to show those provisions in the policy summary.

Medicare.gov’s provider-assignment page explains that a non-participating provider may charge above Medicare’s approved amount when not accepting assignment. That extra is an excess charge. Use Chapter 1’s provider check; ask the billing office and SHIP about your exposure and any applicable state restrictions. This is different from a provider opting out of Medicare entirely.

Plans K and L leave percentages of several covered costs to you. The federal chart shows their annual out-of-pocket limits and explains that full payment of covered services for the remaining calendar year follows meeting both the applicable limit and the annual Part B deductible. Check the current figure for each limit. It is not a limit on premiums or on services the policy excludes.

Plan M pays only part of the Part A deductible shown in the chart. Put the unpaid portion into Chapter 3’s worksheet, where a cheaper premium can be weighed against bills you keep.

Mark two or three candidates. If a lower premium persuades you, write a sentence identifying the expense you’re agreeing to keep.

Three states need a different page

Massachusetts, Minnesota and Wisconsin standardize Medigap differently. Medicare.gov names these exceptions on its basics page and provides a comparison for each state.

If you live in one of them, use Medigap in Massachusetts, Medigap in Minnesota, or Medigap in Wisconsin. Those pages, not a Pennsylvania letter comparison, are your starting point.

For example, Medicare.gov’s Massachusetts comparison separates hospital deductibles, skilled nursing coinsurance and other benefits under state-specific choices. Take the names from your state’s page and ask the company to identify the precise policy and any added coverage in its quote.

State variation also matters beyond these three states. Medicare.gov directs readers to their State Insurance Department for additional buying or switching protections under state law. Don’t infer those protections from a neighbor’s experience across a state line. Ask which rule applies to your residence, age and proposed change, and have the counselor identify the current state guidance.

Find the date beside MEDICAL

The federal Medigap Open Enrollment Period lasts six months. Medicare.gov says it begins with the first month in which you are both at least 65 and enrolled in Part B. This is a buying protection tied to your own circumstances, not a season printed on every calendar.

During that period an insurer cannot use your medical history to deny you a policy it offers or raise your price because of pre-existing health problems. You still pay the policy’s premium. The protection concerns access and health-based pricing; it does not make all letters cost alike or freeze your premium for life.

Count whole months. Someone already 65 whose Part B begins July 1 has a July-through-December window. An October start gives that person October through March. Crossing into a new year doesn’t restart the count.

If Part B starts later than 65, the Medigap clock starts when those two conditions first meet. Whether delaying Part B was safe belongs to Chapter 8’s employer-coverage check, not to a sales conversation about a supplement.

If you already have Part B through disability before 65, reaching 65 supplies the age condition for this federal window. Before 65, Medicare.gov says federal law generally does not require companies to sell you Medigap; state law may provide rights. Take an under-65 question to your State Insurance Department rather than applying the ordinary age-65 shopping advice early.

There is one more qualification to the protected window. Medicare.gov’s buying guidance says coverage can start without a general wait, but allows an exception for coverage related to a pre-existing condition. If a company proposes a pre-existing-condition wait, ask it to count your prior creditable health coverage: at least six continuous months before applying during this window bars that exclusion; shorter creditable coverage reduces it. Ask for the condition, credit and policy effective date in writing. This health-coverage test is not Chapter 4’s creditable drug coverage; the two words travel together and mean different things. A right to purchase and payment for a particular condition are distinct questions.

Use the date printed beside MEDICAL on your Medicare card, together with the month you reach 65. If the resulting window is open, don’t put the decision off until an October advertisement reminds you about Medicare.

When the six months are behind you

Medical underwriting means the insurer evaluates your health information when deciding whether to accept you and on what terms. Medicare.gov warns that after open enrollment you may face higher prices, fewer options, or denial if you do not meet the company’s requirements.

That is the risk in the laptop illustration. Savings can pay a bill today; they cannot create a protected application next year. I’m not telling you to buy a premium you cannot sustain. I’m telling you that waiting is a decision about future access as well as this month’s money.

The six-month federal period doesn’t repeat each fall. Chapter 3’s annual plan-change dates do not require a Medigap company to accept you. Nor does finding a cheaper company’s policy mean that company must sell it to you on the same terms.

But a closed window is not automatically a closed case. Medicare.gov describes separate Medigap protections: rights to buy specified policies without a health-based refusal in qualifying circumstances. Additional state rights may apply. The policies available and the conditions depend on the particular protection; don’t treat the phrase as permission to buy every letter whenever you like.

Medicare.gov’s explanation of how Medigap works gives two relevant trial-right examples. If you dropped Medigap to try Medicare Advantage for the first time, there is a single 12-month trial period to return to your former policy if the company still sells it. If it doesn’t, certain other policies may be available, subject to the applicable rules.

Separately, if you joined Advantage when first eligible for Part A at 65 and return to Original Medicare within the first year, Medicare.gov describes a right to buy certain Medigap policies sold in your state. That age-and-first-eligibility condition matters. It isn’t a fresh trial right after every Advantage enrollment.

If either example fits, take the enrollment dates and notices to SHIP promptly. For a voluntary trial-right return, ask SHIP about applying as early as 60 days before Advantage coverage ends and no later than 63 days after it ends; keep the disenrollment notice and proof of prior coverage. Confirm the specific right and dates before switching. Returning to Original Medicare inside that first year does not leave the application open indefinitely afterward. Confirm coordinated coverage dates with the insurers before giving up existing coverage.

A health-based refusal, an approaching deadline, or a proposed switch after your protected window is where I’d involve a SHIP counselor and, if needed, a state-licensed insurance agent. The agent can handle company-specific applications; ask which insurers they represent. Your State Insurance Department can clarify state protections. The reason for the call is practical: the right letter is of little use if the application cannot be accepted.

A quote you can keep paying

Chapter 3 already put the supplement premium into your household total. Here, make sure the figure is an official quote for your actual application, not just the estimate on Medicare.gov.

The agency’s cost page says premiums depend on the insurer, policy and residence; discounts and underwriting can affect the price. Ask which assumptions and discounts the quote includes. Compare what you’d actually pay.

Ask how the company sets premiums and what can cause increases. Medicare.gov cautions that premiums typically rise each year. Choosing the same benefits from a lower-priced insurer is sensible; assuming today’s price will last for the rest of retirement is not a budget.

For an existing standardized policy, Medicare.gov says health problems do not prevent its automatic renewal. That protection does not stop premium increases, excuse unpaid premiums, or erase the consequences of an untruthful application. Keeping a policy and applying to a different company are different transactions. Don’t cancel the first on the strength of an estimate for the second.

The letter-and-date checklist

Use this alongside the official comparison, with one sheet per candidate. In Massachusetts, Minnesota or Wisconsin, substitute your state’s policy names for letters.

  1. Record your residence, age and Part B start date. Write the beginning and end of your six-month window. If it has passed, have SHIP identify any applicable federal or state protection before you rely on a quote.
  2. Copy the exact plan letter or state-specific name. Label standard, high-deductible or SELECT explicitly. Confirm first-eligibility restrictions if you are considering C or F.
  3. Mark the official chart’s hospital deductible, hospital cost-sharing and skilled nursing rows. Write each amount or portion the candidate leaves to you.
  4. Mark the Part B deductible, coinsurance and excess-charge rows. For N, check the office and emergency-visit copayments. For K or L, record the current limit and its conditions.
  5. Check foreign emergency benefits if you need them. Keep excluded expenses, such as dental work and long-term care, outside the policy’s protection when you budget.
  6. Obtain official quotes from more than one company selling the same choice. Record monthly premium, discounts, pricing assumptions and the date. Ask about future increases.
  7. Ask about medical underwriting, any pre-existing-condition waiting period and the effective date. If a protection applies, confirm the evidence the company requires and its deadline.
  8. Put the quote and residual expenses into Chapter 3’s budget. Keep prescription coverage on Chapter 4’s separate sheet. For a couple, do the calculation for each person.
  9. Read and retain the company’s policy summary. Resolve unanswered questions with SHIP, the insurer or your State Insurance Department before changing coverage. Keep written acceptance and coverage dates with your records.

Start with the card, not the brochures. Copy the Part B date onto the checklist tonight. If those six months are running, give the page a place where it won’t disappear under the mail.

Chapter 6: The Tax Return Behind the Premium

The notice says your Medicare premium is higher. The tax return on the desk is from two years ago, and your pay has changed since then. Those two facts can both be true at once.

The extra amount is called the income-related monthly adjustment amount, shortened to IRMAA. The name is longer than the idea: if your income on the tax record Social Security uses is above a published line, you pay an additional monthly amount for Part B, Part D, or both, depending on the coverage you have. It is not a bill for a service you used. It is not the Part D plan’s own premium. And a lower income today does not, by itself, change the return already used to set this year’s amount.

That last part is what makes the notice feel personal. The system is looking backward while your household is living forward.

Which income, and which year

Social Security’s Medicare premiums page says it uses the most recent federal tax return the IRS provides. Its measure is modified adjusted gross income, or MAGI: adjusted gross income plus tax-exempt interest. This is not simply the amount of money that came into your bank account, and it is not the number at the top of a pay stub.

For the 2026 Medicare premium year, SSA says it generally uses the return filed in 2025 for tax year 2024. In some cases, SSA may have the 2023 return instead. The two-year lookback is a useful rule of thumb, not a reason to ignore the year named in your own notice. Find the tax year SSA actually used before trying to explain the calculation.

If SSA used 2023 for your 2026 premium but you filed a 2024 return, or did not have to file one for 2024, call SSA or visit a local Social Security office and ask it to update the tax year used.

A household can cross an income line for a reason that no longer exists. A person may have worked a full year before retiring. A spouse may have died. An asset sale or another taxable event may have raised the return’s MAGI. The premium notice does not know that the paycheck stopped in January; it uses the tax information sent to SSA. The right response depends on whether the old return is accurate and whether a qualifying event has since lowered income.

IRMAA is individual to the Medicare premium decision, but the income bands depend on tax filing status. A joint return is compared with joint thresholds. A person filing as an individual is compared with the individual schedule. Married people who filed separately and lived with their spouse at any time during the tax year have a separate, much narrower schedule. Do not use that special schedule just because the words “married filing separately” appear on a return; confirm the living-situation rule on SSA’s current page.

The 2026 brackets, in one place

The following are the 2026 amounts published by Social Security. The income ranges use MAGI from the tax return SSA applies. Part B’s listed figure is the monthly surcharge added to the standard Part B premium. Part D’s is the separate monthly income-related charge added to the premium of your drug coverage. The plan’s own Part D premium still varies by plan.

For people filing an individual return, and married couples filing jointly, the schedule is:

  • MAGI of $109,000 or less for an individual, or $218,000 or less jointly: no IRMAA surcharge.
  • More than $109,000 through $137,000 for an individual, or more than $218,000 through $274,000 jointly: Part B surcharge of $81.20 per month; Part D surcharge of $14.50 per month.
  • More than $137,000 through $171,000 for an individual, or more than $274,000 through $342,000 jointly: Part B surcharge of $202.90 per month; Part D surcharge of $37.50 per month.
  • More than $171,000 through $205,000 for an individual, or more than $342,000 through $410,000 jointly: Part B surcharge of $324.60 per month; Part D surcharge of $60.40 per month.
  • More than $205,000 but less than $500,000 for an individual, or more than $410,000 but less than $750,000 jointly: Part B surcharge of $446.30 per month; Part D surcharge of $83.30 per month.
  • $500,000 or more for an individual, or $750,000 or more jointly: Part B surcharge of $487.00 per month; Part D surcharge of $91.00 per month.

SSA also publishes a distinct schedule for certain married people who file separate returns. Whether it applies depends on whether the spouses shared a home during that tax year:

  • MAGI of $109,000 or less: no IRMAA surcharge.
  • More than $109,000 but less than $391,000: add $446.30 monthly to Part B and $83.30 to Part D.
  • $391,000 or more: the monthly additions are $487.90 for Part B and $91.00 for Part D.

These are the surcharges, not the complete premium. For Part B, add the applicable surcharge to the standard Part B premium for 2026 shown in Chapter 1. If you have Part D coverage, add its surcharge to that plan’s premium; the surcharge is not a substitute for the plan premium. If you do not have one of those kinds of coverage, SSA says you pay an IRMAA only for the benefit you do have. For example, a Part B enrollee without Part D does not acquire a Part D charge merely because the tax return falls in a higher band. If your notice adds a Part D adjustment but you have no Medicare drug coverage, call 1-800-MEDICARE to correct the coverage record CMS sends SSA.

The top line on the separate-return schedule is not identical to the top individual or joint line. SSA lists a slightly different Part B add-on there for 2026. Don’t copy one household’s notice onto another person’s worksheet and assume the filing status matches.

SSA may collect the additional amount from a Social Security payment. Its page says that if the charge is greater than the monthly benefit, or if you do not receive a monthly Social Security payment, you may receive a separate bill from CMS or the Railroad Retirement Board. The collection method does not change what the notice is saying. It is still worth checking the underlying income year and filing status before you accept the result as correct.

The brackets and surcharges are not permanent household thresholds. SSA publishes the schedule for each premium year, and the amounts can change. Use its current official table when planning for 2027 or any later year. Don’t carry a 2026 number forward because it happens to be printed in this chapter.

A lower income can matter, but the route has rules

Retirement is the life change people ask about first. Stopping work can qualify for a new decision when it lowers the income SSA uses. The word “retired” by itself is not a pass through a lower premium. SSA needs a qualifying event and information showing the income change.

Its Form SSA-44, titled Medicare Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount—Life-Changing Event, is the route to ask SSA to make a new determination after certain events. SSA lists these life-changing events:

  • You married, divorced, or had a marriage annulled, or your spouse died.
  • You or your spouse stopped working or reduced work hours.
  • You or your spouse lost income-producing property because of a disaster or another event beyond your control.
  • Your or your spouse’s employer pension plan stopped or was reorganized.
  • You or your spouse received a settlement from an employer because the employer closed, went bankrupt, or reorganized.

The event must connect to lower income under SSA’s rules. A planned retirement may fit when work stops and income falls; deciding to retire while income stays above the applicable line does not automatically change the calculation. A market decline, a difficult medical year, or the fact that a premium is uncomfortable is not, by itself, one of the listed events. Read the current form instructions before you send anything.

Form SSA-44 asks what happened and requests information and evidence for SSA to review the change. Follow its current instructions for estimating income and documenting the event. Keep a copy of the completed form, the notice, supporting papers, and the date you sent them. If a letter or employer record establishes the stop-work date, include it as directed by the form. Do not mail your only copy of a document you may need again.

This is a request for a new determination because circumstances changed; it is different from saying SSA used the wrong information. If SSA relied on an incorrect tax return or MAGI, SSA’s page directs you to correct the information with the IRS when the IRS data itself is wrong. If you amended a return and the amendment changes MAGI, send SSA the amended return and the IRS acknowledgment according to its instructions. If you disagree with SSA’s decision for another reason, the appeal route is separate: SSA identifies an online appeal and Form SSA-561-U2, Request for Reconsideration. Check the notice and SSA’s current instructions for the right path and deadline.

A tax professional can help if you cannot confidently estimate MAGI after a complicated sale, pension event, amended return, or employer settlement. That professional can help with the tax calculation; SSA decides how the IRMAA rules apply. For questions about the Medicare premium notice itself, use Social Security’s official number or local office, and keep the notice in front of you when you call. A SHIP counselor can also help you understand the Medicare side without selling a plan.

The surcharge is separate from the plan decision

IRMAA does not change a drug plan’s formulary or make one insurer’s plan fit your prescriptions better. Chapter 4’s comparison still needs the same medicines, strengths, quantities, and pharmacy. Put the Part D surcharge on its own line beside the plan premium so it does not disappear from the household estimate or get mistaken for a plan benefit.

The same separation helps with Part B. Chapter 1 explains the standard Part B premium and deductible; the IRMAA amount is an added premium charge determined by income. It does not replace the deductible or coinsurance. If you have both Part B and Part D, you can see two income-related amounts. If you have only one, SSA says its adjustment applies only to the coverage you have.

The surcharge also does not decide when to claim Social Security. Claiming age is a separate decision; IRMAA is based on the tax information and premium-year rules SSA applies. The larger claiming strategy belongs in Social Security, Claimed On Purpose, not in this chapter’s arithmetic.

If you are thinking about a tax move because of a Medicare premium, pause before acting. A change to income can affect taxes and other parts of a household’s finances, and a Medicare chart alone cannot tell you whether a conversion, sale, or withdrawal is wise. Ask a tax professional to model the consequences before you make an irreversible transaction. This book can help you read the premium notice; it cannot replace tax advice.

A notice-and-life-change checklist

Set the notice beside the tax return rather than trying to reconstruct the story from memory. Use this checklist for each person who received a determination.

  1. Write down the premium year, the Part B amount, any Part D amount, and the tax year SSA says it used. Compare the notice with SSA’s schedule for that exact premium year.
  2. Check filing status and the MAGI line. Remember SSA’s definition: adjusted gross income plus tax-exempt interest. For an MFS return, check the household-status qualification in SSA’s current instructions before selecting a bracket.
  3. Decide which problem you have. If the IRS return or SSA’s income information is wrong, follow the correction or appeal instructions. If the tax information was accurate but a qualifying event later lowered income, read Form SSA-44. For a Part D surcharge despite having no drug-plan enrollment, ask CMS to correct its coverage record at 1-800-MEDICARE; SSA receives that record from CMS.
  4. If the notice uses tax year 2023 for 2026 premiums, contact Social Security when you filed for 2024 or had no 2024 filing requirement; ask the agency to update its record.
  5. Match the event to SSA’s list. Record its date and how it changed income; gather the evidence the current form requests. Stopping work can be relevant, but retirement alone does not settle the request.
  6. Complete the form using its current instructions and keep the full submission, evidence, and mailing or upload confirmation. Note any response date SSA gives you.
  7. If you cannot calculate the income estimate, ask a tax professional. If the notice or Medicare coverage question is unclear, call SSA or a SHIP counselor rather than relying on a sales pitch.
  8. Put the next premium-year table check on your calendar. Check SSA’s current IRMAA page and Medicare.gov before using any 2026 amount for a later year.

Take out the notice now and circle the tax year printed on it. That date is the first thing to verify.

Chapter 7: The Application Worth Sending

Marcus’s message arrived on a Tuesday, while the library table was still empty. His mother was paying for prescriptions and had decided the help programs were for people with no income at all. He had helped her look at the official rules, then sit down with an application. She qualified for Extra Help. Her drug costs dropped.

That is the whole story, and it is enough. No miracle, no exact savings figure to promise you. A program helped because somebody checked the rules instead of guessing from the name.

The two programs in this chapter answer different bills. Extra Help lowers certain costs for Medicare Part D prescription coverage. Medicare Savings Programs, run by states, can pay some Part A and Part B costs. A person may qualify for one or both. The income and resource tests change. For MSPs, states may use more generous rules than the federal baseline. I won’t give you a number to carry into another year. Medicare.gov’s current pages show the limits for the year they apply to; check the current figure before deciding you are over it.

This is not the high-income surcharge from Chapter 6 turned upside down. It is a separate eligibility check, with its own agencies and paperwork.

Extra Help follows the drug bill

Medicare.gov calls Extra Help a program for people with limited income and resources who need help with Part D costs. Depending on the current rules and your coverage, it can help with a plan premium, deductible, coinsurance, and copayments for covered prescription drugs. It can also protect you from the Part D late-enrollment penalty while you receive the help.

The details that matter at the counter still depend on your drug plan and the prescription. Chapter 4’s formulary and pharmacy checks remain useful: Extra Help does not make an uncovered medicine covered, and it does not tell you which plan fits your list. Check the current Medicare.gov drug-cost page and the plan’s information for the year you are choosing. If the amount at the pharmacy doesn’t match your Extra Help notice, call the plan or 1-800-MEDICARE while you still have time to sort it out before a refill runs out.

Some people get Extra Help automatically. Medicare.gov says that includes people with full-benefit Medicaid, people whose state pays their Part B premium through a Medicare Savings Program, and people receiving Supplemental Security Income from Social Security. If one of those applies, watch for the official notice. It may tell you how much you pay and, if you do not already have Part D coverage, which drug plan Medicare has selected for you.

Do not file the notice under “junk” just because you didn’t fill out an Extra Help application. Read the plan name, effective date and instructions. If a plan was selected for you, compare it against your current prescriptions and pharmacy. Chapter 4 explains that comparison; this chapter’s point is to make sure the help and the coverage are both actually in place.

If you are not automatically enrolled, you can apply through Social Security. The application and current instructions are at SSA.gov’s Extra Help page. You can apply online or ask Social Security about other application methods. Keep a copy of what you send and any confirmation. For help understanding the questions, a SHIP counselor can walk through the Medicare side without selling you a plan.

The application asks about financial circumstances under the rules in force. Don’t rely on a neighbor’s old limit, an article without a year, or an online calculator that doesn’t name its source. Medicare.gov says Extra Help limits can go up each year. Its page also explains which income and resource figures apply, including separate treatment for Alaska and Hawaii. Check the current year and the rules for your state before you rule yourself out.

That is one reason applications get abandoned in the kitchen drawer. A person sees a limit, counts every dollar in the wrong way, and decides the answer is settled. The official application instructions are the place to check what counts. If a pension, property, or unusual account makes the answer hard to calculate, ask Social Security or SHIP how to proceed rather than inventing a formula.

The state programs pay different parts of the bill

Medicare Savings Programs, or MSPs, are administered by state agencies. Medicare.gov says they can help with Part A or Part B premiums; some categories can also help with deductibles, coinsurance and copayments for Medicare-covered services. The state decides which program fits after you apply. A Medicare card does not tell you whether the state has finished that decision.

There are four federal program names on Medicare.gov. They are not four labels for the same benefit.

  • The Qualified Medicare Beneficiary program, or QMB, can pay the Part B premium, Medicare cost-sharing for covered Part A and Part B services, and a Part A premium if you owe one. Medicare.gov says providers may not bill a QMB enrollee for Medicare-covered deductibles, coinsurance or copayments. Keep proof of QMB status with your Medicare card and show it when you receive care. The protection concerns covered Medicare services; it is not a promise that every service or bill is covered.
  • The Specified Low-Income Medicare Beneficiary program, or SLMB, helps pay the Part B premium. Medicare.gov says you need both Part A and Part B to qualify under this category.
  • The Qualifying Individual program, or QI, also helps pay the Part B premium for people who meet its rules. Medicare.gov says QI applicants must apply each year, and states approve applications on a first-come, first-served basis, with priority for people who received QI the prior year. Check the current state process and funding before assuming last year’s approval automatically continues.
  • The Qualified Disabled and Working Individuals program, or QDWI, can pay a Part A premium for a narrower group: people with a disability who are working and lost premium-free Part A and certain Social Security disability benefits after returning to work. If that description might fit, ask the state to review the situation; don’t try to decide from the program name alone.

The exact eligibility requirements and monthly income and resource limits are on Medicare.gov’s Medicare Savings Programs page. They change over time. The federal page lists separate limits by program and household size, with different figures for Alaska and Hawaii. It also warns that some states may allow eligibility above the federal figures or disregard certain kinds or amounts of income and resources. The federal number is a starting point, not a ruling on your state’s application.

A person can have too much for one category and still be eligible for another. The benefits are not identical, either. QMB is the broadest of these descriptions for Medicare cost-sharing; SLMB and QI focus on the Part B premium; QDWI addresses the Part A premium in its specific working-and-disability circumstances. Let the state determine the fit rather than trying to squeeze your household into a label before applying.

Why the word “resources” stops people

Income and resources are separate parts of these tests. The program may not treat every dollar or asset the way you expect. The rules can differ by program, state and year. A balance on a bank statement, a home, a vehicle, a retirement account, and money coming in monthly are not interchangeable entries on a worksheet. Don’t assume all count; don’t assume none count.

The helpful question is not “Am I poor enough?” It is “Which current rule does my state use for this program, and what documents does it need from me?” That’s a more answerable question. Medicare.gov links to state Medicaid contacts for the application and local criteria. If you live in Alaska or Hawaii, use the relevant state-specific figures. If the state page doesn’t explain an item you own or receive, ask the state office before excluding yourself.

It may be tempting to use a broad income number from a tax return as a substitute for the program’s test. Resist that shortcut. The IRMAA calculation in Chapter 6 uses a specific tax measure and lookback; it is not the application rule for these programs. The Social Security Administration and state Medicaid agency can tell you which documents their process requires. A tax return may be one document, but it is not a universal stand-in for the full eligibility decision.

A denial is not a reason to guess at a new number or quietly give up. Read the reason, the date and the instructions for asking the state to review or appeal. If your income changed, your household changed, or you think an item was counted incorrectly, ask what evidence the agency will accept and what deadline applies. A SHIP counselor can help identify the Medicare piece; a state eligibility worker is the person to ask about the state’s calculation. If a complicated property or income question affects several benefits, a qualified benefits counselor or attorney may be appropriate because the consequences can reach beyond Medicare.

Put both applications on the same page

Medicare.gov says you can apply for Extra Help and a Medicare Savings Program at the same time. Its current guidance says Social Security can send information to the state to start an MSP application unless you tell it not to on the Extra Help application. That handoff is a convenience, not proof that the state has all it needs or has approved you. Watch for a request from the state and answer it by the stated deadline.

For Extra Help, Social Security is the application route. For an MSP, your state Medicaid office makes the eligibility decision. One phone call to the wrong office can leave you with a referral and no application, so be clear about which program you are asking about. If you want to check both, say so.

A person who qualifies for an MSP that pays the Part B premium may also qualify automatically for Extra Help under Medicare’s rules. Even then, read the notices. Automatic eligibility for assistance does not mean you can ignore the Part D plan name, the pharmacy rules, or the start date. Some people are automatically placed in a drug plan if they don’t already have Part D coverage. Check the plan against your medicines and ask Medicare or SHIP about a change if something does not fit.

Keep the documents together: the Extra Help application confirmation, any request from the state, the approval or denial notice, and the plan’s drug-cost information. Write down the name of the person you spoke with, the date, and what they asked you to send. Paperwork has a talent for becoming three separate stories in three separate envelopes.

The limits belong to the current year

The 2026 and 2027 information on the official sites is not a permanent eligibility chart. Medicare.gov says MSP income and resource limits rise each year and notes that states can be more generous. It says Extra Help limits may also increase. Those pages are better than a chart clipped from an old benefits packet, but even a federal page needs its year checked before you apply.

Do not use last year’s denial as proof you cannot qualify this year. Your income or resources may have changed; the limits may have changed; and the state may count an item differently than you expect. Medicare.gov specifically encourages people who are unsure about MSP eligibility to apply. If your circumstances sit close to a limit, that is a reason to get the current rules, not a reason to round your way out of the program.

If you are helping a parent, ask permission before collecting financial papers or submitting anything. Let the person read the notices and keep a copy. A relative can help organize a file without taking over the decision. Marcus helped his mother get through the process; the application was hers, and the result came from the program’s review.

The eligibility-check worksheet

Use one copy for each person. Fill it from official sources, not memory. Leave a blank if you cannot verify an answer; that blank is a question for the agency.

  1. Write the date, state of residence, household size and the person applying. Note whether the question is about Extra Help, an MSP, or both.
  2. Check whether full-benefit Medicaid, SSI, or an MSP paying the Part B premium may already qualify the person for Extra Help automatically. Look for a notice and confirm the status with the agency if it is unclear.
  3. Open Medicare.gov’s Extra Help page. Record the eligibility-limit year, the income and resource figures for the applicant’s household, and the source date. If it is not the current year, stop and find the updated information.
  4. Open Medicare.gov’s MSP page and copy the current limits for each category that might fit. Mark the relevant state link and check for state rules that disregard income or resources or use higher limits.
  5. List the program-specific help: Part D plan costs and penalty protection for Extra Help; Part A or Part B premiums and, for some MSP categories, Medicare cost-sharing. Do not write “all medical bills” in the margin.
  6. Apply for Extra Help through Social Security. Contact the state Medicaid office to apply for an MSP, even if you also submitted an Extra Help application.
  7. Keep copies, submission dates and confirmation numbers. Calendar any document deadline or renewal date in the decision notice, especially an annual QI application.
  8. When a decision arrives, record the effective date, program name, what it pays, what remains yours, and any next review date. If it is denied, follow the notice’s review instructions and deadline.
  9. If the numbers or documents are confusing, ask the agency that decides that program. Use SHIP for Medicare questions and a qualified benefits professional when a difficult income or asset question may affect several programs.

A rule in a book can point you toward the door. It cannot decide what the state counts in your case. Open the current Medicare.gov limits today, then make the call or start the application before the envelope slides back under the stack.

Chapter 8: The Paycheck, the Health Plan, and Part B

The payroll form is already filled out. A box is checked beside the Health Savings Account, and the employer adds money each payday. Then a Medicare card arrives in the mail, and suddenly two reasonable choices seem to collide: keep the job plan, or sign up for Medicare.

This is not one decision. It is three: who pays first, whether you need Part B now, and what Medicare enrollment would do to HSA contributions. The answers depend on the kind of coverage you have and whose current work provides it. The number of people employed by the company matters, too.

Don’t let a general rule made for someone else’s workplace settle this for you. Ask the benefits administrator to explain your specific plan in writing, and check the current Medicare and IRS guidance before you sign up or keep contributing to an HSA.

Start with who pays first

Medicare and an employer group health plan can both cover you, but one generally pays before the other. That order affects whether the job plan will pay its share if you don’t enroll in Part B.

CMS’s Medicare Secondary Payer guidance says that for someone 65 or older with a group plan tied to their own or a spouse’s active job, employer size generally determines the payer order. At an employer with at least 20 employees, the group plan generally pays first and Medicare second. Below that threshold, Medicare generally pays first and the group plan second.

That difference is practical, not merely bookkeeping. When Medicare is primary and you haven’t enrolled in Part B, the employer plan may calculate its payment as though Medicare had paid first. You could be left with costs you thought the job plan would cover. With a qualifying plan from a larger employer, the group coverage may be primary, which can make delaying Part B an option for some people. It is still not an automatic recommendation.

CMS describes this as a high-level summary of payer rules. Multi-employer arrangements and unusual work situations can complicate the count, and other Medicare eligibility circumstances can have different coordination rules. Ask the benefits office which employer’s plan covers you, how the employer counts for Medicare coordination, and which insurer is primary. If the answer is unclear, contact Medicare or the Benefits Coordination & Recovery Center before relying on it.

Ask for the plan’s current Summary of Benefits and the section explaining coordination with Medicare. A card in your wallet proves that you are enrolled in the employer plan; it does not tell you whether the plan expects Medicare to pay first. If the benefits office gives you a verbal answer, send a short email repeating what you understood and ask them to correct it if needed. Keep that reply with the plan papers. You want an answer you can show the claims office later, not a memory of a phone call made between meetings.

The plan’s label won’t answer the question. A benefits administrator can tell you how the plan is designed to coordinate with Medicare; Medicare can confirm enrollment rules. Ask both sides. Keep names, dates and the answer in writing.

Four questions before you choose

First, ask, “Who pays first if I have Medicare and this plan at the same time?” Get the answer for your exact coverage. When Medicare is primary, ask what the plan will pay if you delay Part B. When the group plan is primary, ask whether its benefits remain the same after you become Medicare-eligible. The plan document and benefits office should settle the details, not a colleague’s story from another company.

The second question is whether you are still covered because you or your spouse is actively working. Coverage that continues after a job ends is a different thing. Chapter 2 explains the Special Enrollment Period for Part B: the working-coverage window and its deadline are tied to current employment and group coverage ending. Use that chapter for the complete timing and paperwork. Here, the working decision is simpler: don’t mistake a retiree plan, COBRA, or an individual policy for active-employee coverage that preserves that same enrollment route.

The third question is what happens to the rest of the household if you change coverage. A spouse may be on your employer plan, or you may be covered through a spouse who is still working. Ask whether enrolling in Medicare or leaving the group plan changes the spouse’s eligibility, premium, or enrollment rights. Ask what happens to a dependent still on the policy. Get the effective dates. A choice that works for you can create a gap or a higher bill for somebody else if the household rules are different from what you assumed.

The fourth question is whether an HSA changes the calendar. This is the part that catches people who believe they can sign up for Part A and keep contributing to the account because they’re still at work. The IRS says Medicare enrollment makes the contribution limit zero for the affected months, including months covered retroactively. Part A can start retroactively when some people enroll after 65, so the month you apply may not be the first month that matters.

Part A and the HSA calendar

An HSA is not the same as a regular savings account with a tax-free label. You can generally keep and spend money already in the account for qualified expenses, but Medicare enrollment blocks new contributions for the covered months. That includes money from your employer as well as payroll deductions.

The IRS’s current Publication 969 explains that HSA eligibility ends with Medicare enrollment and that retroactive coverage counts. Medicare.gov says premium-free Part A can, in some cases, begin as much as six months before the date a person signs up, but no earlier than the month they turned 65. That makes the enrollment date and the coverage-effective date two different dates to check. If you have an HSA, do not treat the application date as a safe cutoff by itself.

For example, imagine someone still working at 67, covered by a high-deductible employer plan, and contributing to an HSA. They plan to apply for Social Security benefits in November and then learn that Medicare enrollment may begin retroactively. Medicare.gov advises you and your employer to stop HSA contributions six months before you retire or apply for Social Security or Railroad Retirement Board benefits. If Medicare backdates Part A coverage, contributions made for covered months may exceed the allowed amount. The surprise does not come from a new contribution in November; it can reach back into earlier payroll deposits. This is a made-up calendar illustration, not a claim about a particular worker’s eligibility or tax result.

Before applying for Part A, ask Social Security what start date would apply in your case and ask your HSA administrator or tax professional how to handle contributions around that date. If you plan to enroll, coordinate with payroll and the employer so contributions stop when they should. If contributions have already been made for a month that later turns out to be covered by Medicare, don’t guess at a fix or assume the employer can simply reverse it. Ask a tax professional how to review the contributions, correction options and tax reporting under the current IRS instructions.

The HSA balance stays. The payroll deposits may have to stop months before you apply for Medicare; get both dates on paper before you give payroll an instruction. The question is whether the employer coverage and HSA contributions are valuable enough to keep delaying Medicare, given the payer order, the coverage you need, and the deadline that will apply when employment ends.

If you already receive Social Security benefits when you approach 65, check any Medicare enrollment notice and the effective date on the card rather than assuming you are still outside Medicare. Enrollment can happen automatically in some circumstances. An HSA payroll contribution that continues after Medicare enrollment can create a tax problem even when nobody meant to make a mistake.

A spouse’s job can be your bridge, but check the bridge

People often say, “I’m covered through my spouse, so I can wait.” That can be right, but the useful details are whose employment provides the group coverage, whether that spouse is still working, and how large the employer is for Medicare’s payer rules. CMS includes a spouse’s current employment in its working-aged coordination guidance. If the coverage comes through a retired spouse, it is not the same active-employment situation.

Ask the employer to put four things in a letter or benefits email: whether the policy is based on current employment; the employer-size category used for Medicare coordination; whether the group plan pays before or after Medicare; and what event ends the coverage for you. Ask whether your spouse’s continued employment maintains your coverage if you personally retire. Then ask what happens if your spouse retires first. A family plan can have two retirement dates and two Medicare decisions, even if the insurance card has one policy name.

Do not assume that a plan which pays first will stay unchanged once you enroll in Medicare. Ask about the plan’s coordination rules, how claims are submitted, whether the plan expects you to have Part A or Part B, and what it pays if you do not enroll. Medicare.gov explains that if an employer or retiree plan is secondary, you may need Part B before it pays. Confirm the answer for the plan you actually have.

If you are leaving work, put the last day of employment, the last day of group coverage, and the requested Medicare start date on the same page. Chapter 2 owns the full eight-month Special Enrollment Period explanation; its clock is not a reason to wait until the last minute. Gather proof of employer coverage and ask the benefits office to complete the employer section of Form CMS-L564 if required for your application. Medicare.gov’s ready-to-sign-up instructions describe the forms and where to send them. If you have railroad employment, follow the Railroad Retirement Board’s instructions instead of assuming the Social Security process is identical.

This is also the moment to bring in help. If the employer’s written answer conflicts with what the insurer tells you, call Medicare or the Benefits Coordination & Recovery Center and ask how to verify who pays first. A SHIP counselor can help you compare the Medicare side without selling a plan. A tax professional should review HSA contributions or retroactive coverage because excess contributions can affect your return. If an employer plan is changing your spouse’s coverage, ask the benefits administrator before you submit a Medicare application or drop anyone from the policy.

The decision list

Write the answers down for yourself and any spouse or dependent on the plan. Leave a blank where the employer has not confirmed something; a blank is a question, not a yes.

  1. Whose active work supplies the insurance? Write your employer or your spouse’s employer, the coverage end date, and whether this is active-employee coverage rather than retiree or continuation coverage.
  2. Who pays first? Record the employer-size category and the primary payer confirmed by the benefits administrator. If the workplace is small or uses a multi-employer arrangement, ask specifically how it coordinates with Medicare. If there is disagreement, verify with CMS or Medicare.
  3. What would Part B change? Ask for the employee and spouse premiums, deductibles, cost-sharing, provider access, and any effect on dependents. Ask for the employer’s current written notice stating whether its prescription coverage is creditable for Part D; keep it and compare its end date with the Part D enrollment instructions in Chapter 4. Medicare.gov warns that a gap of 63 days or more without Part D or creditable drug coverage may cause a penalty. Compare the whole household coverage, not just the premium deducted from your pay.
  4. Is there an HSA? Set a stop date for deposits from both sources no later than six months before planned retirement or an application for Social Security or RRB benefits; that is Medicare.gov’s guidance. Ask Social Security or RRB which Part A effective date applies, then have a tax professional review the tax-year contribution limit before you instruct payroll. Record the Part A and Part B dates, including any retroactive Part A month. Include employer money in the review; it counts toward HSA contributions.

Then make one phone call with the list in front of you. Ask the benefits office to confirm its answers by email. Ask Medicare or Social Security about your enrollment window and effective date, not whether your employer plan is “good.” If an HSA is involved, ask your tax professional to check the calendar before you apply. The right next step may be enrollment now, or it may be a carefully documented delay while you keep working. It depends on the coverage and dates you actually have.

Take the benefits letter and your HSA statement out tonight. Mark the expected retirement or Social Security/RRB application date on the calendar and identify the six-month HSA cutoff Medicare.gov specifies. Before making a payroll change, verify the Part A start date with Social Security or RRB and have a tax professional check contributions for the year.

Chapter 9: The Numbers to Check Every Fall

The pencil is beside the open book, and the official page is open on the screen. That is the right time to find a number that has changed: before you use last year’s figure to choose this year’s coverage.

This is a reference chapter, not another tour of Parts A, B, or D. Most dollar figures below were printed earlier; the 2026 Part D national base premium is added for penalty checks. They are a dated snapshot, not a promise about what you will pay in another year. Use the blanks to keep the year, the updated amount, and the page you checked together. A number without its year is a number waiting to mislead you.

Three places to check

Start at Medicare.gov’s Medicare costs page. It separates Part A and Part B from Advantage, Part D, and Medigap. For Part A and Part B, find the current-year premium and deductible sections. Read the smaller cost-sharing entries too; do not assume the daily amounts stayed put because the main premium looks familiar.

For prescription coverage, use Medicare.gov’s Part D costs page. Check the cap for covered Part D drugs, the maximum deductible a plan may set, and the base beneficiary premium if you are reviewing the late-enrollment-penalty calculation. A plan may set a lower deductible or none, so the federal maximum is not a quote for a particular plan.

For IRMAA, open Social Security’s Medicare premiums page. Choose the schedule for the premium year you are checking, then match the filing status and income range on your notice. The added Part B amount and the separate Part D amount belong beside the right band; do not copy a neighbor’s line or use a prior-year schedule because the tax return looks similar.

CMS and SSA release yearly cost information in the fall, but release dates vary. Mid-to-late October is a pattern, not a promised deadline, and different figures can appear on their official pages at different times. CMS’s Newsroom carries official announcements and fact sheets; Medicare.gov and SSA.gov are where you should confirm the amount that applies to your coverage.

I checked these pages on October 4, 2026. Medicare.gov’s general costs page and SSA’s IRMAA page displayed 2026 amounts. Medicare.gov’s Part D page already displayed the 2027 cap and deductible maximum: $2,400 (2027) and $700 (2027). Those are the 2027 Part D figures available on the check date, not estimates. Reopen the pages before acting; a later official update takes precedence over this dated note.

The pencil update list

The dollar-update lines start with dated amounts; items 3 and 8 separately identify rules to verify rather than annual price resets. Fill the current-year box from the official page, and record the date you checked it. If the source does not yet show the year you need, leave the box blank and check again before enrolling or relying on a cost estimate. Do not carry a prior-year number forward just to complete the page.

If you keep this page for next year’s review, write a new amount in a dated column rather than erasing the old one. Note what changed: a premium, deductible, daily cost, or income-related addition. Keep a saved official page or printout with the entry, and mark an unavailable figure “not yet shown” rather than leaving it ambiguous. That small trail lets you compare years without mistaking an estimate for an official amount.
