  2. Part A deductible: $1,736 per benefit period (2026). Current amount: _____. Official source and date checked: _____.
  3. Part A inpatient hospital daily amounts: $0 for days 1-60 after the deductible, $434 per day for days 61-90, and $868 per day for days 91-150 while using lifetime reserve days (2026). Current daily dollar schedule: _____. Separately verify the lifetime-reserve rule: 60 days total during your lifetime, not a fresh allotment each year. Rule source and date checked: _____.

The Part D 2027 amounts shown above are already published as of October 4, 2026. Do not treat that as proof that every other 2027 figure has been released. For Part A and Part B premiums and deductibles, and SSA’s 2027 IRMAA bands, write down what the official page says on the day you check it. If the page still shows 2026, the honest entry is “not yet shown” plus the date; revisit the page later. Never fill an empty space with a guess.

A 2027 renewal, checked on paper

For example, suppose a reader has a 2027 renewal notice and a prescription list. Enter the published 2027 Part D limits, use that year’s Plan Finder with the actual medicines and pharmacy, and mark unpublished Part A/B or IRMAA figures “not yet shown” with the check date.

Keep the Plan Finder estimate beside the plan’s Evidence of Coverage, not instead of it. Confirm the same plan year, medicines and pharmacy in both, then record the plan name and date checked. A maximum federal deductible is a ceiling for what a plan may set, not the amount every plan charges. If a missing federal number could change the choice, ask Medicare or a SHIP counselor what can be confirmed and set a date to revisit the official page.

Keep the source page or a saved copy with the worksheet. When you return to check an amount, compare its label and year with the blank you are filling; a fresh page can still display a prior-year figure. If a plan document and Plan Finder do not appear to agree, confirm the plan name and coverage year before comparing the drug list again. Ask the plan to explain a plan-specific cost; ask Medicare or a SHIP counselor about a federal cost or enrollment choice. Write down the answer and the date, so next fall you can tell a changed rule from a different plan estimate.

When a covered prescription costs more at the counter than the month can bear

The heating bill and a large prescription can arrive in the same week. The voluntary Medicare Prescription Payment Plan lets a Part D enrollee, including someone with Advantage drug coverage, pay eligible prescription costs through monthly plan bills rather than at pickup. Medicare.gov’s Before using this payment option explains that participation has no fee or interest and does not lower the total owed. Your plan premium remains separate.

The public page describes the monthly calculation this way: this month’s eligible prescription costs plus the unpaid balance from the previous month, divided by the months remaining in the calendar year. New fills change the balance, so the payment need not stay fixed. Use the plan’s billing estimate and actual statement for the amount due; the formula is not permission to send a self-calculated payment.

One dated example is enough to see the scale. Medicare.gov’s 2026 April example combines a regular prescription costing $4 with a one-time prescription costing $613: $617 of out-of-pocket drug costs in April 2026. The person elects participation before those fills. Spreading that April expense alone across April through December gives a rough average of $68.56 for each of nine months in this 2026 illustration. It is not the official installment schedule: recurring refills add costs, and the plan recalculates its bills. Compare the plan’s expected April payment with the cash you would otherwise need at pickup, not with a promise of nine identical bills.

Use one enrollment-and-exit checklist:

  1. Before the large fill, request participation through your health or drug plan. Record its confirmation, effective timing, first expected bill and due date. Do not assume the pharmacy has received an election the plan has not approved.
  2. Compare the schedule with the household’s available cash, keeping premiums outside it. Joining after September leaves fewer months and may offer little timing relief. If the total is unaffordable, check Chapter 7’s assistance programs rather than treating installments as a discount.
  3. Check each statement against the fills and carried balance. Medicare.gov directs billing-error grievances to the process in your Member Handbook or Evidence of Coverage. Its Using this payment option page says to pay the regular plan premium first to protect drug coverage.
  4. To leave, contact the plan. New eligible costs return to pharmacy payment; the existing balance can be paid at once or billed monthly. Changing health or drug plans ends the old participation, so elect again with the new plan if wanted. The previous plan’s balance still belongs to that plan.
  5. If a payment is missed, use the date in the reminder. Failure to pay by that date removes you from the payment feature, not from the underlying health or drug plan; the balance remains due without interest or fees.

Drug coverage belongs to Chapter 4: use its formulary, restriction and pharmacy guidance for that question. If the plan denied coverage, follow the appeal instructions in its written decision; Chapter 3’s ‘When the plan says no’ section explains the appeal routes.

The pages and dated example were checked October 4, 2026. Verify the later coverage year’s program instructions with your plan before using this reference; no 2027 installment amount is promised here.

Put the check date beside the amount

Write the premium year and the date you opened SSA’s schedule above the number you copied; for every other entry, record its coverage year, official source and check date. Check available 2027 plan documents now, verify pending agency amounts when published, and do not let the October 15-December 7 plan-change window pass while waiting for a missing figure. Ask a SHIP counselor to review a choice affected by a pending amount.

If the official pages disagree with your notice

For an unexpected Part B or Part D premium, first identify the premium year, the coverage you have, and any income-related amount on the notice. Then compare those lines with the current CMS or SSA page. A plan’s own Part D premium is not the same entry as the Part D IRMAA addition. If the amount still does not make sense, call the agency named on the notice and ask which year and data it used. Keep the notice, your worksheet and the call date together.

If an IRMAA notice appears to use the wrong tax information or a year that does not fit, return to Chapter 6’s routes: a data correction, a request tied to a qualifying income-changing event, or an appeal are different matters. SSA decides the IRMAA determination. A tax professional can help when the tax record or a complicated transaction needs review; a SHIP counselor can help with the Medicare coverage side. Bring the notice and the relevant official schedule. Do not rely on an agent’s estimate to resolve a Social Security determination.

The book carries 2026 amounts because those were the verified published values used for the Part A, Part B and IRMAA discussions. Its 2027 title names the enrollment season, not permission to invent 2027 figures. Part D is the exception in this dated check: Medicare.gov had published its 2027 cap and maximum deductible by October 4, 2026. As other official numbers become available, the page that publishes them, rather than a printed prediction, gets the last word.

Put the notice beside the official schedule. Circle the year on each before you copy a number.

The Date on the Calendar

The first thing I would do with this book is close it.

Not because the subject is finished. Because the next useful thing is not another page. It is a date written where you will see it.

Medicare decisions have a way of making ordinary people feel they ought to become experts before they can make one sensible choice. You do not. You need a clear question, the current official page, and the patience to stop when the answer belongs to your own file. Worry will not tell you whether the notice applies; the dated notice and the agency that issued it might.

A date, not a season of dread

Medicare.gov lists October 15 through December 7 as the yearly Open Enrollment period for reviewing and changing certain coverage. Mark the October 15, 2026 start, or verify the next applicable start if you read this later; keep the dated answer behind your choice in the folder beside that calendar.

Let a good decision be good enough

No one can know every future health expense, every change in a household, or every adjustment a program will make. That is not a reason to freeze. It is a reason to make the best decision the available evidence supports, preserve the documents behind it, and return when something material changes or the next annual review comes around.

You’ve checked what you can. Keep the answer you got, and put the pencil down.
